How do environmental factors influence jogging behaviour across large-scale, small-scale and informal green spaces? A comparative study and sustainable renewal strategy of multi-type green space systems based on crowdsourced data
abstract: Jogging constitutes a crucial pathway linking urban green spaces and human health. Although their positive association is well-established, how variations in green space scale and type influence jogging remains insufficiently understood, particularly in high-density urban contexts. This study addresses this by analyzing 2,031,479 crowdsourced jogging records in Beijing to compare the associations between environmental factors and jogging behaviour across large-scale, small-scale, and informal green space type paths. The findings reveal that while large-scale green space type paths has the highest jogging frequency per path, small-scale and informal green space type paths form a broad jogging network, collectively accounting for 65.7% of all jogging activity. Regression models show that greater water coverage, higher rubber rate, lower path length are positively associated with jogging frequency and path completion rates in all path types. Crucially, several associations are inconsistent, challenging a “one-size-fits-all” planning approach. For instance, more green spaces are linked to higher completion rates in small-scale green space type paths, but lower rates in informal green space type paths. Higher tree coverage is significantly associated with higher total jogging frequency and path completion rates only in small-scale green space type paths. Drawing on these findings, this study proposes a context-dependent multi-scale green space renewal framework. This provides planners and policymakers with evidence-based tools to design jogging-friendly environments for sustainable healthy cities.

title: Participatory agent-based scenario development for mid-sized cities: Evaluating housing and sustainable mobility interactions
abstract: • Participatory ILUT modelling applied in a mid-sized North American city • Four-unit zoning plus parking limits reduce car dependence most • Agent-based model captures spatial and income travel heterogeneity • Scenario design co-developed with planners for policy relevance . This study explores the interplay between housing supply strategies, specifically greenfield and infill developments, and long-term changes in car ownership, travel mode choices, and vehicle/passenger kilometres travelled in the context of mid-sized North American cities. The City of Moncton serves as a representative case study, having recently experienced rapid internal and international migration. Particular focus is given to the emerging four-unit zoning strategy, currently being deployed in several Canadian provinces, as a means to address rising housing demand. An agent-based integrated land use and transportation (ILUT) modelling framework is applied to project population and behavioural dynamics from 2021 to 2046 under multiple land use and housing development scenarios. These scenarios were co-produced through an iterative collaborative process involving practising planners and engineers from the City of Moncton and the DalTRAC research group. The ILUT framework was developed using the 2023 CanTRAC survey data through calibration of discrete choice and heuristic behavioural models, with further validation of model outputs against the 2016 and 2021 Canadian Census data. Validation results indicated close agreement, with mean absolute error below 3% and root mean square error below 5%. Simulation outcomes revealed that while infill development alone does not sufficiently reduce car dependency, the combination of four-unit zoning with residential parking restrictions yields a significant reduction in car ownership and fosters a shift toward active modes of travel. These findings offer actionable insights for policymakers and planners aiming to shape sustainable mobility in rapidly growing mid-sized cities.

title: “It’s fair once you’re in it” - Comparing public and government perceptions on Zero Emission Vehicle policy
abstract: Public support is important for policy success, and people tend to be more supportive of policies they perceive to be fair. Where public perceptions were not adequately considered, or where the views of the public and government diverge, policy outcomes may be different than expected. However, there is only very limited research on public perceptions of fairness, particularly in transport. Drawing from the tenets of a Just Transition, this study examines public acceptability and perceptions on a major UK decarbonisation policy: The Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) Mandate which, at the time of data collection, required all new cars and vans sold in the UK to be zero emission from 2035 onwards. Public perceptions were studied in ten workshops with members of the public, and captured in causal loop diagrams. These findings are compared with the UK government’s policy texts and consultation reports, and with an interview with government officials. The Government’s consultations around the ZEV Mandate focussed on the industry impacts and the mechanisms for managing the scheme. The impacts of the policy on the public were marginalised. Citizens raised concerns over procedural and recognition justice. Whilst the benefits of transitioning were noticed, the system was clearly seen to privilege those who already had good jobs, access to finance and own their own homes - those who are already seen to do well. The research reveals that the inevitable tensions on who wins and loses at different points in a technology transition are not considered, risking to undermine the public acceptability of the measures.

title: Spatial heterogeneity of driving factors for urban heat islands and carbon emissions: Decoding priorities, thresholds, and synergistic interactions
A CFD-CONTAM-BES framework incorporates wind pressure, air temperature, and indoor air circulation to estimate energy consumption of high-rise buildings
Data-driven risk assessment of climate-related failures in railway infrastructure
abstract: Climate-related failures pose increasing risks to railway operation and maintenance, requiring robust assessments to support effective resilience planning. Accordingly, this study presents a comprehensive risk assessment to identify, quantify, and prioritize climate-related failure modes (CRFMs). CRFMs were identified through text mining of 15-year corrective maintenance records across all five Swedish railway regions. A probabilistic model was then developed to analyze the risk of identified CRFMs, considering both operational and maintenance costs. Risk distributions were derived using Monte Carlo simulation and summarized by Expected Value of Risk (EVoR) and Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR 0.90 ). As a result, 14 CRFMs were identified, accounting for 47% of all failure records. Their annual trend and seasonal distribution align well with periods of increased extreme weather events and dominant seasonal climate hazards. Furthermore, clustering the regional profile of CRFMs reveals regional similarity. The CRFMs were then prioritized, showing that 4 modes (i.e., Track deformation, Snow and ice, Buckling, and Rail breakage/crack) account for 73% of total CVaR 0.90 . The amplification of total risk in the tail indicates a 74% higher cost burden under extreme conditions. Finally, regional climate vulnerability was assessed using risk metrics normalized by track length and traffic density.

title: Development of a comprehensive multi-criteria decision support system for assessing the environmental and cost impacts of buildings
Spatial patterns of supply–demand and network resilience in urban emergency services: A multi-system case study of Shijiazhuang, China
Estimation of spatiotemporal changes in electricity-related greenhouse gas emissions in South Korea using nighttime light data
From data to impact: Lifecycle-oriented digital twins for urban heat island mitigation and climate resilience
Graph-driven urban structure analysis: Typology inference and performance linkage from VHR imagery
Deciphering the impacts of urban gray–green spaces on seasonal diurnal land surface temperature in a valley-basin city via explainable machine learning
Physics-informed neural network calibration and application for urban cooling
abstract: Mitigating the adverse effects of urban heat islands (UHI) is essential for enhancing climate resilience, public health, and energy sustainability in cities. Traditional modelling approaches, however, often face a trade-off between physical fidelity and the flexibility to integrate diverse geospatial data. This paper presents a novel physics-informed neural network (PINN) framework that bridges this gap by embedding the heat diffusion equation directly into a neural network, ensuring predictions adhere to thermodynamic principles while learning from complex urban data patterns. It includes a systematic data-fusion workflow that unifies multi-format geospatial inputs, such as land surface temperature (LST), vegetation indices, and vector-based urban morphology, into a cohesive gridded structure, enabling scalable and reproducible urban climate analysis. Validated through a case study of Paris, the model achieves strong predictive accuracy (MAE=0.3723 °C, RMSE = 0.5019 °C) and captures the city’s thermal patterns with consistent error across the observed temperature range. Comparing two targeting metrics, LST and the proposed urban heat thermal index (UHTI), shows that LST favors areas with some existing vegetation while UHTI identifies more barren, structurally vulnerable zones. Simulated green roof deployment on buildings selected by each metric yields localised surface cooling up to 4.97 °C, concentrated on the building footprints. This integrated approach thus serves as a practical scenario planning tool, quantifying the relative benefits of green infrastructure. By combining physical simulation with data-driven analytics, this research provides urban planners and policymakers with a scientifically rigorous, scalable resource to support the design of cooler, and more sustainable cities.

title: Integrated AI framework combining routing, computer vision, and large language models to assess urban park access disparities among people with and without mobility impairments
Action-oriented urban agriculture opportunity spaces: Prioritization, sustainable-development potential, and food self-sufficiency rates
Moving beyond exposure: a globally comparable framework for heat risk assessment in cities
Impacts of the built environment features and comprehensive experience on adaptive behavior in the context of climate change: A partial least squares structural equation modeling approach
abstract: Under the combined pressures of global climate change and high-density urbanization, public open spaces (POSs) are critical infrastructure for enhancing urban resilience. However, current "one-size-fits-all" design paradigms often fail to meet users' adaptive needs. To bridge this gap, this study proposes a replicable theoretical and analytical framework, which integrates spatial type, built environment, individual background, comprehensive experience, and adaptive behavior to quantify how environmental features drive differentiated adaptive behaviors. Validating this framework using Lhasa, China, as a test-bed site, the study identifies spatial types through multi-source data fusion and cluster analysis. Furthermore, it systematically verifies hypothesized pathways using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Multi-Group Analysis (PLS-MGA). Empirical results confirm the robustness and interpretability of the framework. While the core psychological cognitive process: "attitude to perception to willingness to adaptive behavior of spatial" remains universal, the framework sensitively captures the "context dependency" of the drivers behind adaptive behavior. Additionally, the study clarifies that the built environment exerts an indirect regulatory effect through psychological mediators, rather than acting as a direct physical determinant. Consequently, this study advocates a paradigm shift from "standardized supply" to "precision support." By providing a scalable research framework, this study empowers policymakers and urban planners to formulate context-aware and resilient spatial governance strategies. These strategies can adapt to diverse geographical and cultural contexts.

title: Understanding multi-perspective urban green space patterns under urban expansion: Evidence from Guangzhou
How do underground pedestrian systems in a railway transition hub area sustainably mitigate pedestrians exposure to extreme heat? A case study in Tenjin, Fukuoka, Japan
Neighborhood walkability and intergenerational mobility: Uneven associations across space and race
Cooling accessibility of urban parks: Unraveling spatial disparity and nonlinear drivers using an improved polynomial-2SFCA model and explainable machine learning
A multi-stage ROM-enhanced CFD-ML framework for efficient 3D urban wind-field prediction
Artificial intelligence-related technologies for municipal solid waste management: A review and new insights from smart cities
Exploring changing determinants of lake cooling effects on urban heat island in a rapidly urbanizing area
Cities as thermodynamic systems: unpacking political power, governance capacity, and structural inequality in the production of urban sustainability
Optimization of cross-regional dispatching for shared autonomous electric vehicles considering charging and carpooling constraints
When dense built-up areas cool: Multi-scale neighborhood pattern changes of a semi-arid urban cooling paradox in Tehran (2000–2020)
abstract: In semi-arid cities such as Tehran, declining urban green space and expanding Built-Up areas are typically assumed to intensify surface heating. However, long-term observations suggest that several districts may have experienced cooling within the Built-Up fabric, while green spaces have lost part of their expected influence. This paradox indicates that conventional assumptions about vegetation’s thermal advantage may not fully explain semi-arid urban dynamics. The novelty of this study lies at analyzing Built-Up cooling dynamics in Tehran by integrating two decades (2000 – 2020) of land use change and urban green space (UGS) dynamics parameters with cooling indices for land surface temperature (LST) of urban green spaces (TUGS) and LST of Built-Up areas (TBU), evaluated across several buffer distances in 22 districts. False discovery rate (FDR) controlled correlations of TUGS and TBU with, morphological, demographic, and atmospheric variables were analyzed to evaluate the cooling efficacy of the TBU and TUGS indices. Results showed a notable green space loss in several districts, with per - capita provision declining by up to 125%, while surface LST in parts of the built up fabric fell by roughly 0.7 – 2.8 °C. TUGS weakened across many districts, with reductions of 0.3 – 0.6 units at 100 m and up to 1 – 1.5 units at 300 – 500 m, whereas TBU shifted by about 1 – 2 units in mid-range buffers toward stronger relative cooling. Lower sky - view factor (SVF) generally aligned with enhanced cooling, while greater horizontal / vertical density and human pressure were associated with reduced cooling capacity. Bivariate color mapping revealed scale - dependent and increasingly heterogeneous cooling patterns, with Built-Up morphology playing a more prominent role at larger buffer distances over time. Collectively, these patterns suggest that thermal behavior in semi - arid cities may be non - linear, with Built-Up areas under certain configurations exhibiting cooling comparable to, or occasionally exceeding, that of green spaces.

title: Corrigendum to “Multisensory Urban Climate Zones (MUCZ): A Framework for Mapping Dynamic Multidomain Human Comfort in Complex Urban Fabrics beyond Urban Morphology” [Sustainable Cities and Society, Volume 131, September 2025, Article 106673]
Housing conditions as drivers of pediatric sleep disparities in U.S. cities
abstract: Any vision of urban sustainability is incomplete without a commitment to human sustainability, yet many urban environments often create conditions that compromise children’s sleep. These environments shape disparities in pediatric sleep health through multifaceted pathways, with socioeconomic and housing conditions serving as major drivers. Housing not only reflects socioeconomic status but also mediates children’s sleep environments and their exposure to extreme weather events. However, urban-scale assessments of sleep disparities remain scarce due to limited population-level data on sleep health and environmental exposures. This study introduces the SLeep and Environmental Exposure evaluation framework for urban Populations (SLEEP), a bottom-up approach for assessing urban sleep health disparities in response to climate events (i.e., wildfire smoke) across 13 U.S. cities. SLEEP is further validated by comparing its results with sleep-related indicators from an independent nationwide dataset. Our results reveal substantial variation in pediatric sleep outcomes across cities, primarily driven by housing conditions. Children living in multifamily dwellings, overcrowded households, and rental units face elevated risks. Physical housing characteristics emerge as key determinants. These findings demonstrate how housing conditions amplify children’s vulnerability to climate stressors, reinforcing sleep health disparities rooted in broader socioeconomic disadvantages.

title: Navigating trade-offs in urban nature restoration: Spatial prioritization of brownfield greening for supporting multiple targets of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework in a high-density city
abstract: Brownfield greening (BG) offers a strategic spatial opportunity to support the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) in urban contexts, particularly Target 2 on ecosystem restoration. However, how different spatial prioritization strategies for pursuing this restoration objective may influence other urban-relevant targets, such as Target 11 (nature’s contributions to people) and Target 12 (urban greenspace access), remains underexplored. This study developed six brownfield greening scenarios based on different planning objectives and prioritization logics and assessed their contributions to selected KMGBF targets in Guangzhou, a high-density city in China. The results suggest markedly different spatial outcomes across scenarios. Based on the scenario comparison, human-centered targets (Targets 11 and 12) were more often advanced together, whereas connectivity oriented restoration (Target 2) was less consistently aligned with these human centered targets. Among the tested scenarios, a balanced efficiency scenario provided a useful intermediate pathway, retaining over 80% of the maximum tested performance for Targets 11 and 12 while maintaining approximately 60% of the highest observed connectivity gain for Target 2. Overall, this study offers a scenario-based planning framework for exploring how alternative BG strategies may support selected KMGBF targets in land-constrained cities. By making potential trade-offs and synergies more explicit, the framework can inform biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning (Target 1), support more transparent urban restoration decision-making, and facilitate public communication and participation in restoration planning (Target 14).

title: Quantifying functional criticality of lifelines through mobility-derived population-facility dependence for human-centered resilience
abstract: Lifeline infrastructure underpins the continuity of daily life, yet conventional criticality assessments remain largely asset-centric, inferring importance from physical capacity or network topology rather than actual behavioral reliance. This disconnect frequently obscures the true societal cost of disruption, particularly in underserved communities where residents lack service alternatives. This study bridges the gap between engineering risk analysis and human mobility analysis by introducing functional criticality, a human-centered metric that quantifies the behavioral indispensability of specific facilities based on large-scale visitation patterns. Leveraging 1.02 million anonymized mobility records for Harris County, Texas, we operationalize lifeline criticality as a function of visitation intensity, catchment breadth, and origin-specific substitutability. Results reveal that dependence is highly concentrated: a small subset of super-critical facilities (2.8% of grocery stores and 14.8% of hospitals) supports a disproportionate share of routine access. By coupling these behavioral scores with probabilistic flood hazard models for 2020 and 2060, we demonstrate a pronounced risk-multiplier effect. While physical flood depths increase only moderately under future climate scenarios, the population-weighted vulnerability of access networks surges by 67.6%. This sharp divergence establishes that future hazards will disproportionately intersect with the specific nodes communities rely on most. The proposed framework advances resilience assessment by embedding human behavior directly into the definition of infrastructure importance, providing a scalable foundation for equitable, adaptive, and human-centered resilience planning.

title: Enhancing pedestrian thermal comfort in subtropical cities: an integrated spatiotemporal analysis of tree morphology and route planning
Grey–green urban drainage performance and resilience under rainfall variability: An optimal coverage framework for Quito (Ecuador)
abstract: Climate variability combined with rapid urbanization and population growth is increasing pressure on urban drainage systems, amplifying flood risks and associated impacts on public health and the urban environment. To support evidence-based decision making in this context, this study presents an optimal coverage assessment framework to evaluate the performance and resilience of grey–green and hybrid urban drainage systems under spatio-temporal rainfall variability. The proposed framework integrates reliability, resilience, and sustainability concepts to jointly assess system exposure to rainfall stressors and its hydraulic response. Natural threats are represented through design storms associated with multiple return periods, extreme rainfall events derived from continuous time series, and plausible rainfall extreme events, while system response is quantified using key hydraulic indicators obtained from hydrodynamic simulations, including runoff generation, flood volumes, and network surcharging behavior. A multi-objective optimization approach is applied to identify the optimal spatial extent of green stormwater management practices, explicitly accounting for performance gains and land-use constraints. The robustness of policy-relevant outcomes is ensured through a multi-criteria decision analysis that enables transparent comparison of alternative infrastructure configurations. The framework is demonstrated through its application to the urban drainage system of Quito (Ecuador), a representative case of rapidly growing cities in complex topographic and climatic settings. Results show that hybrid grey–green configurations consistently outperform conventional systems, achieving high resilience levels, particularly in flood mitigation, despite requiring a limited allocation of urban space to green infrastructure. Overall, the proposed framework offers a transferable and decision-oriented tool to guide urban planners and policymakers in prioritizing resilient and sustainable stormwater management strategies under climate uncertainty.

title: URBANPEDIA as an interactive design dictionary: A quantitative morphological approach for walkability
Summer peaks, overheating, and excess deaths by 2100? The energy and health system impacts of space cooling in a changing climate
abstract: Climate change is increasing global temperatures, with implications for indoor overheating, cooling energy demand, and public health. This study uses a validated agent-based model of residential energy use to assess the impacts of climate change on residential space cooling in Aotearoa New Zealand, modelling eight representative neighbourhoods across the socioeconomic spectrum in Auckland and Christchurch, the two largest cities. In the highest-temperature scenario (SSP5-8.5 in 2081-2100), space cooling could shift the national electricity system from winter to summer peaks, while lower-temperature scenarios (SSP2-4.5 and/or shorter time horizons) do not switch overall peak demand seasonality. Without adequate adaptation, indoor overheating could increase annual cardiovascular mortality by up to 6.4% in the highest-temperature scenario, which would disproportionately affect low-income and other vulnerable populations. These effects are lesser, but still present, in SSP2-4.5 and shorter time horizons. Increased heat pump adoption mitigates health impacts but increases electricity demand and infrastructure costs, with an average 610,000 NZD of additional costs per excess life saved. These findings highlight the need for integrated energy and health policy responses, including equitable access to cooling, building design reforms, and proactive infrastructure planning, and the need to address both energy justice and system resilience to minimise harms across society.

title: Principal component analysis and fuzzy clustering for neighborhood-scale urban morphology-based thermal hazard assessment
abstract: Urban heat islands pose significant public health concerns, yet neighborhood-scale thermal assessment faces data limitations. Satellite-derived surface temperatures inadequately reflect pedestrian-level thermal exposure, while sparse meteorological networks cannot resolve intra-urban heterogeneity. Morphology-based approaches address this gap by using urban form characteristics as physical determinants of local thermal conditions through their influence on ventilation, shading, and heat storage. However, morphological indicators are inherently correlated, causing multicollinearity, and conventional classifications impose rigid boundaries that misrepresent transitional zones where thermal conditions vary gradually. This study develops a framework combining Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) clustering to address both challenges. The framework is applied to Warsaw, Poland, using nine urban morphology variables computed at 10m resolution with a 310m neighborhood analysis window, with strict multicollinearity control (VIF<10). PCA extracted two significant components (eigenvalues>1) explaining 65.6% of variance: PC1 (43.3%) represented the urban-natural gradient, while PC2 (22.3%) distinguished water-influenced zones from vegetated areas. FCM clustering on the PCA scores identified nine distinct morphological typologies. A novel membership transformation approach aligned fuzzy membership degrees with relative thermal patterns derived from averaged Landsat surface temperatures (summer 2019-2025), orienting values toward thermal hazard magnitude rather than cluster proximity. The highest-risk cluster (compact mid-/high-rise built-up areas, mean LST=36.0°C) was further stratified into five thermal hazard classes, revealing high building density (BCR=0.56) and minimal vegetation (0.5%) in Very High hazard zones. The framework provides actionable information for targeted heat mitigation while quantifying classification uncertainty in transitional zones, offering a generalizable approach for cities with adequate morphological data.

title: Learning from residuals: a knowledge-data-driven hybrid model for explaining the social-ecological influences on urban agglomeration resilience
What heats cosmopolitan cities in summer? A remote sensing and AI study of land surface temperature drivers: Casablanca vs Barcelona
abstract: Urbanization and climate change are increasingly intensifying the urban heat island effect, especially during summer, by changing the relationship between land cover and local thermal conditions. This study investigates how five environmental indicators (NDVI, NDMI, NDBI, NDBSI, and albedo) influence land surface temperature (LST) across Local Climate Zones (LCZs) in two cities with contrasting climates and urban forms, Casablanca and Barcelona, during the summer period (July 1–August 31) from 2014 to 2024. Landsat 8 imagery and the WUDAPT database were combined with seven machine-learning regression models. Among these, the Extra Trees Regressor demonstrated the strongest performance, achieving the highest R² values (0.96–0.98 in training and 0.59–0.85 in testing), the lowest error metrics, and the best bias, and was therefore selected to assess the contribution of each predictor by LCZ class and year. Results show that vegetation, represented by NDVI, plays a leading role in regulating LST in Barcelona, with the highest feature importance values (0.30–0.40), consistent with its Mediterranean setting. In Casablanca, thermal variability is more strongly associated with urbanization-related indicators, particularly NDBI and NDBSI, with feature importance reaching 0.57. In addition, Barcelona exhibits a statistically significant upward trend in summer LST, with mean Sen’s slopes of 0.31°C/year in built LCZs and 0.34°C/year in land-cover LCZs, according to the Mann–Kendall test. Casablanca shows a comparatively more stable thermal pattern. These findings highlight that LST–environment relationships depend on both LCZ structure and regional climate, providing insights for urban heat mitigation and climate-adaptation strategies.

title: The Chalcedony and Nephrite Corridor: Enhancing blue and green infrastructure to cool the city
Attribution analysis of spatial mismatch between flood risk and public response: Insights from geospatial explainable artificial intelligence framework
Assessing future heat stress risk across Swedish residential areas using a combined GIS and indicator-based approach
abstract: Sweden's housing stock, designed predominantly for winter thermal performance, is increasingly exposed to summer heat extremes following record heatwaves in 2014, 2018, and 2022. Despite projections of intensifying heat risk and the near-total absence of mechanical cooling in Swedish residential buildings, no prior study has delivered a nationally comprehensive, indicator-based compound risk assessment integrating hazard, exposure, and vulnerability at the municipal scale. This study addresses that gap through an integrated framework covering all 290 Swedish municipalities, combining GIS-based climate data processing, standardised Poisson regression for empirical indicator selection, and CA-Markov land cover projections under RCP 2.6, 4.5, and 8.5 scenarios to 2040. Thermal hazard is characterised through maximum seasonal air temperature, consecutive summer days, and tropical day frequency derived from UERRA-HARMONIE reanalysis and SMHI regional projections; vulnerability is constructed from seven demographic, socioeconomic, and built environment indicators; and exposure is represented by SCB municipal population forecasts. The composite index is externally validated against observed 2018 excess summer mortality across all 290 municipalities, with the equal-weighted specification outperforming PCA- and regression-beta-weighted alternatives (Pseudo R² = 0.117, p = 0.007); the index is interpreted as a spatial prioritisation tool rather than a mortality prediction model. The 2040 projections are framed as a counterfactual stress test, applying projected thermal forcing to a fixed sociodemographic baseline. Results identify a pronounced south-north risk gradient, with Stockholm, Göteborg, Malmö, Burlöv, and Solna remaining persistently classified as high risk under every scenario. By 2040, over 230 of 290 municipalities are reclassified to medium risk or above, driven primarily by committed demographic ageing rather than emissions pathway, with RCP 2.6 and RCP 8.5 producing near-identical patterns. Elderly fraction, low-income share, building density, and vegetation proximity emerge as the significant mortality predictors, providing an evidential basis for spatially targeted adaptation centred on green-blue infrastructure, equity-oriented cooling access, and differentiated heat-health warning systems.

title: How does the synergy of digital empowerment and green transition enhance urban energy resilience: Quasi-natural experimental evidence from China’s dual policy pilots
Urban greening as a potential nature-based solution for heat-related health burden: Evidence from acute myocardial infarction in a megacity
Energy communities for low-carbon and resilient urban energy systems: a distributed framework for sustainable urban energy transitions
Semantic behavioral sequences from UAV video: Decoding the effects of the micro-scale built environment on human behavior in neighborhood centers
abstract: Understanding how neighborhood centers support behavioral processes in everyday routines is important for clarifying their contribution to sustainable neighborhood development. Such behavior is diverse, context-dependent, and often unfolds as continuous processes organized around goals and needs, calling for a person-centered behavior mapping paradigm. Yet recording such processes at the micro-scale without losing behavioral semantics, and transforming them into comparable and analyzable evidence, remains challenging. To address these challenges, this study uses semantic behavioral sequences as an analyzable representation of behavioral processes, preserving behavioral semantics while enabling standardized cross-site analysis. Using unmanned aerial vehicle footage from 43 neighborhood centers, the study integrates computer vision to infer behavior across human–environment and social interaction dimensions, sequence analysis to identify typical behavioral patterns, and manual annotation to quantify environmental features. Statistical models then test how these features and their interactions relate to site-level pattern proportions. Three behavioral patterns are identified: task-oriented, unplanned interaction, and active stopping. The models reveal distinct built-environment associations across patterns, along with significant interaction effects between function and design. This study proposes a semantic behavioral sequence framework that makes behavioral processes computable and offers a new methodological pathway for environment–behavior research. The findings provide actionable insights for targeted spatial interventions and precision design in neighborhood centers.

title: Evaluating the collective effects of vertical and ground greening on microclimate and energy consumption in a high-density building array
Energy-logistics mutual feedback driven multi-agent dynamic interactive game model for low-carbon ports: Towards synergistic improvement of energy utilization and logistics management efficiency
A hybrid MCDM integrating XGBoost and explainable AI to assess urban ecosystem resilience and identify contributors: A case of Chinese cities
Differentiated street greenery cooling of road surfaces: Spatially varying nonlinear effects from street view and geographically weighted machine learning
abstract: Urban vegetation is a critical nature-based solution for mitigating the urban heat island effect, yet its cooling efficacy on road surfaces varies spatially due to differences in vegetation type, structure, and local urban morphology. This study investigates the spatially varying nonlinear cooling effects of differentiated street greenery, including trees, shrubs, and grass, on land surface temperature (LST) using Google Street View (GSV) imagery in Zurich, Switzerland. A fine-tuned Mask2Former deep learning model was employed for semantic segmentation to accurately extract five street view factors (trees, shrubs, grass, buildings, and sky) from GSV images collected via three methods: multi-view collection, panoramic image collection, and fisheye. These factors were then compared across methods, revealing methodological biases but limited influence on subsequent modeling outcomes. A geographically weighted random forest model integrated with SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) analysis was developed to capture spatially non-stationary and nonlinear relationships between the five view factors and LST derived from Landsat 8. Results show that trees exert the strongest nonlinear cooling effect, followed by shrubs, while grass provides moderate and context-dependent benefits; buildings consistently drive warming, and sky view has minimal impact. The three GSV collection methods yield comparable predictive performance and feature interpretations, suggesting practical flexibility in method selection. This framework advances street-level urban climate research by combining pedestrian-perspective data with local machine learning interpretability, offering evidence-based insights for targeted greening strategies in heat-vulnerable urban areas.

title: Multi-scenario prediction of future urban heat islands: an integrated 2D-3D spatial morphology-driven approach in Wuhan metropolis
Where if? Using spatial, building-stock-driven simulations to explore construction circularity strategies in Gothenburg, Sweden
abstract: Recycling construction materials can significantly reduce the environmental impact of the construction and demolition sector. However, implementing circularity strategies requires a spatially refined understanding of material stock dynamics. In this study, we introduce a stock-driven and rule-based simulation that forecasts – over space and time – material stocks, flows, and associated embodied carbon resulting from construction, renovation, and demolition activities. It enables the exploration of how urban parameters, such as the recycled content of new constructions, demolition rates, renovation rates, and different types of new construction, influence material flows and embodied carbon. Using Gothenburg’s residential building stock, we demonstrate the simulation's capabilities by tracking eight building materials along with their embodied carbon over time, across the parameters, and for two scenarios: a baseline, and a policy on energy efficiency. The simulation can be expanded to include more materials and built environment assets, facilitating informed decision-making and strategies for a sustainable construction sector.

title: A UAV-based methodology for assessing wind power generation from roof-mounted turbines in urban heterogeneous wind environments
Mapping urban vulnerability to air pollution through an integrated geospatial framework: An analysis of 1000 cities in Iran
The smarts behind electricity: How smart city pilot policy impact electricity utilization performance in Chinese cities?
A Facility-Level Framework to Assess Hospital Seismic Resilience through Interdependent Urban Infrastructure Assessment and Enhancement Strategies
Uncovering potential benefits of sustainable energy and climate action plans in small municipalities in Europe
abstract: The Covenant of Mayors (CoM) has been supporting over 10 000 signatories in their energy and climate transition by providing a flexible and adapted methodological framework. More than 60% of CoM signatories are small municipalities, with a population below 10 000 inhabitants. Despite specific barriers, small local authorities contribute to tackling climate change, even though their contribution might be often underestimated. This study assessed the potential of Sustainable Energy and Climate Action Plans (SECAPs) to be used by small municipalities as a multipurpose central tool bringing additional benefits beyond the expected energy and climate outcomes against three distinct perspectives: Social, Environmental, and Urban and Territorial Management in two timeframes (pre and post SECAP implementation). Results show challenges in isolating the potential contribution of the SECAPs in the social and environmental perspectives, while the findings support the potential role of the SECAPs in innovating municipalities’ urban institutional frameworks.

title: Precision governance for urban decarbonization: Decoupling passenger and freight transport emissions by integrating explainable AI and clustering
Decoding the spatial imbalance of urban green space’s cooling service from a supply-demand perspective: A case study of Xi’an, China
Agglomeration under strain: Nonlinear dynamics of urban functional conflicts
Understanding continuance intention toward electrified vehicles for sustainable and resilient mobility: Integrating VBN and ECT with a user heterogeneity analysis
abstract: Although the adoption of electrified vehicles (EVs) has been widely studied, less is known about their continued use, which is essential for achieving sustainable urban mobility and long-term decarbonization goals. This study integrates Value–Belief–Norm theory and Expectation Confirmation Theory to explain continuance intention among hybrid and battery electric vehicle users, focusing on post-adoption psychological mechanisms that support sustained engagement with electrified mobility. Survey data from 434 Spanish EV owners were analyzed using PLS-SEM, complemented by Pathmox analysis to explore user heterogeneity. The results show that altruistic and biospheric values positively influence awareness of consequences, ascription of responsibility, and personal norms, which in turn enhance expectation confirmation and continuance intention. Expectation confirmation emerged as the strongest predictor of continuance intention, highlighting the critical role of positive usage experiences in consolidating sustainable mobility behaviors beyond initial adoption. The heterogeneity analysis reveals distinct user profiles with different psychological drivers of continued EV use: older and long-distance drivers rely more strongly on stable moral commitments reinforced by satisfactory experiences, whereas younger and newer users are guided more by exploratory motivations or ecological ideals, with weaker dependence on experiential confirmation. These findings underline the importance of moving beyond one-size-fits-all approaches in urban mobility policies and suggest that differentiated communication, infrastructure planning, and user engagement strategies are needed to foster long-term commitment to electrified vehicles as a cornerstone of sustainable city development.

title: Assessment of coupled PV-EV penetration in a grid-connected district energy system with scheduled charging: A case study of a mixed-use district in Northern Italy
Rethinking Urban Cold Spots: Downstream Microclimate and Optimal Placement
Water-Land-Energy-Carbon nexus in cities: A dynamic model with evidence from Beijing
How climate risk drives urban green innovation: Evidence from 292 cities in China
Optimal policy design for urban renewable energy systems: A mathematical modeling approach toward sustainable cities
Identifying CO2 emission reduction strategies tailored to different building types by integrating multi-scale factors via deep learning
Greening guidelines for cooling European neighbourhoods with temperate climate: A research-through-design approach
abstract: Green infrastructure measures such as street tree planting and ground surface greening effectively mitigate urban heat. As heat stress intensifies, identifying effective spatial arrangements of these interventions becomes increasingly important. To provide actionable guidance for real-world projects, practical design and resource constraints must also be considered. However, studies that systematically balance cooling effectiveness with practical applicability remain limited. This study develops design guidelines on the size, amount, and spatial distribution of street trees and grass in urban neighbourhoods, focusing on applicability in urban design practice. Four neighbourhood typologies in temperate-climate European cities were used as case examples, for which multiple greening scenarios were generated. A research-through-design approach was adopted: focus group workshops with practitioners evaluated the scenarios in terms of visual experience, functionality, cost, and maintenance; then the refined designs were assessed using ENVI-met simulations. The refined scenarios reduced mean PET by 1.07–7.89 °C compared with the no-greening reference case, with the strongest reductions in wide-street typologies. However, greater green coverage did not necessarily lead to stronger cooling: in a narrow-street typology with diagonal street orientations, the tree-only scenario reduced mean PET by 1.79 °C, while the tree–grass scenario with higher tree and grass coverage reduced mean PET by 1.33 °C. For each typology, two recommended scenarios are identified: one maximising cooling capacity and one prioritising cooling efficiency under space and resource constraints. By translating thermally ranked scenarios into practitioner-refined greening guidelines, this study provides design support for neighbourhood-scale, morphology-specific heat mitigation through the strategic spatial arrangement of street trees and grass.

title: Rethinking urban inefficient land identification and optimization: A case study in Shenzhen, China
Urban ecological environment quality and brain aging: epidemiological evidence from a middle-aged and elderly population-based cohort
A comparative assessment of sampling strategies for tree-based machine learning models in urban flood susceptibility prediction with imbalanced data
Urban building shadow exposure metric (UB-SEM): Quantification of urban building compactness for cooling energy demand prediction
abstract: Urban morphology greatly influences cooling energy demand in buildings. However, limited understanding and quantification of compactness-related factors such as inter-building shading and solar exposure undermine the accurate prediction of cooling energy demand. This study presents a comprehensive multi-scale framework that integrates geometric, spatial-statistical, fractal, and point-pattern measures to capture urban building compactness and its relationship with cooling energy demand. Central to this framework is the Urban Building Shadow Exposure Metric (UB-SEM), a novel, climate-responsive indicator that quantifies cumulative inter-building shading using sun-path dynamics, building geometry and inter-building spacing. Applied across India’s five climatic zones, UB-SEM demonstrates moderate to strong associations with Cooling Energy Use Intensity (EUI), revealing the influence of climate, sun-path, and building geometries. UB-SEM is further evaluated as a surrogate for surrounding-building effects in Urban Building Energy Modelling (UBEM). When used to approximate radiative interactions, UB-SEM-adjusted Cooling EUI shows high agreement with full-context energy simulations with surrounding buildings’ effects, yielding r = 0.88, R² = 0.78, and a low percentage RMSE of 8.33%. These results demonstrate that inter-building effects can be captured efficiently using a shadow-based compactness indicator like UB-SEM through a simplified formulation. This substantially reduces the need for computationally intensive radiative modelling in many UBEM applications focused on cooling energy demand. The study provides a scalable, transferable, and computationally efficient framework for urban building compactness-energy analysis. By incorporating climate-aware shadow dynamics into compactness assessment, UB-SEM supports efficient UBEM workflows and offers a robust foundation for evidence-based urban design across diverse climatic contexts.

title: Toward interpretable urban spatial layout generation: Encoding domain knowledge into graph neural networks
abstract: While deep neural networks advance urban spatial layout (USL) generation, the uninterpretable nature restricts their practical application in human-value-aligned planning scenarios. This study presents the Hierarchical Causal Graph Neural Network with Domain Knowledge Constraints (HCGNN-DKC). This is a neuro-symbolic model that internalises the ontology and expert priors from the planning domain into the information delivery mechanism, while further regularising the model’s predictive scope through logical rules. Evaluations indicate that HCGNN-DKC significantly outperforms baseline models in performance (average accuracy of 85.2%, recall of 74.1%, MSE of 0.523) and generalisability. Crucially, rule-violation test results and real-world applications prove that the embedded logical rules serve as a safety guardrail, effectively mitigating physical violations. Furthermore, whilst adhering to prior knowledge, the model exhibits an autonomous knowledge discovery capability that transcends expert presets. The semantic proximity shown by our framework provides a vital bridge between planning semantics and spatial modelling, establishing an interpretable and intelligent knowledge-based planning support systems.

title: Quantifying urban heat island effects on building cooling energy use in Hong Kong at high spatiotemporal resolution
abstract: Hong Kong experiences a pronounced urban heat island (UHI) effect with substantial implications for building cooling energy use, yet most existing studies assess UHI-energy relationships at low resolution and do not resolve intra-urban or diurnal variability. This study quantified the impacts of UHI on building cooling energy use in Hong Kong at 1 km spatial and hourly temporal resolution under normal and extreme heat days. The results indicated that nighttime UHI intensity exceeded daytime levels in Hong Kong and intensified during extreme heat days, with hourly peak values reaching up to 4.05 degrees C in the urban core. Correspondingly, UHI-induced increases in cooling energy use were markedly greater at night than during daytime conditions, typically ranging from approximately 1.4% to 12.7% at night compared to 0.3% to 4.7% during the day. Localized nighttime maxima reached 19.2% under normal summer conditions and approached 24.8% during extreme heat days. These findings provide quantitative evidence of UHI-related impacts on building cooling energy use and highlight pronounced spatiotemporal heterogeneity under both normal and extreme heat conditions.

title: A causal GeoAI framework for capturing the unearned increment to self-finance public infrastructure
Corrigendum to “The optimal buffer for urban features to impact outdoor thermal comfort” [Sustainable Cities and Society 131 (2025) 106733]
Three-dimensional thermal benefits of urban tree canopy under calm conditions: a case study in Hong Kong
Urban heat resilience from a state–process perspective: Heatwave-induced cooling service supply–demand mismatch and hierarchical spatial allocation of greening
Nonlinear and interaction effects of 2D/3D urban morphological change on high-temperature-zone expansion in Beijing central districts (2000-2020)
Why do residents still drive and travel beyond high-accessibility neighborhoods? Examining the challenges to the 15-minute city concept
abstract: The 15-minute city concept promotes proximity to essential services as a pathway to more walkable, localized lifestyles. However, proximity may not be sufficient for such behavior, as residents in highly accessible neighborhoods often continue to drive or travel beyond their immediate surroundings. This study uses non-work trip data for trips originating from high-accessibility neighborhoods in Chicago to explore three sets of factors beyond proximity that shape travel decisions: (1) the spatial configuration of amenities, (2) built environment features, and (3) individual and trip characteristics. A novel metric, the “harmony of amenities,” is developed to capture the functional synergy among co-located amenities from empirical co-visitation patterns. The analysis is based on a bivariate probit model that jointly estimates destination choice (within or outside the 15-minute walkshed) and mode choice (walking or driving). Results reveal that while proximity is necessary, it is not sufficient. Pedestrian-oriented urban design features such as sidewalks, parks, and visually compact streetscapes, along with the functional harmony of nearby amenities, trip purpose, and individual characteristics, significantly shape both mode and destination choices. These results underscore the need for a more nuanced approach to implementing the 15-minute city concept, one that moves beyond simply increasing the number of nearby amenities to improving built environment quality, optimizing spatial arrangements of amenities, and integrating behavioral insights.

title: Automated urban energy assessment: From thermal flyover to AI-driven retrofit prioritization for sustainable cities
Sponge cities for a greener future: Assessing the impact of sponge city pilot policy on the synergistic efficiency of pollution and carbon reduction
Multiple driving patterns for the coordinated development of urbanization and flood disasters from a configuration perspective: A dynamic QCA approach
Causal machine learning uncovers thresholds and seasonal reversal in landscape-meteorology-driven urban Heat-PM₂.₅ coupling
abstract: In the context of rapid urbanization, the mutual amplification between the urban heat island (UHI) effect and air pollution has emerged as a severe composite environmental challenge. Most existing studies focus on the linear driving mechanisms of individual environmental issues, leaving a systematic understanding of their nonlinear interactions, seasonal dynamics, and causal pathways largely unexplored. To address this gap, this study focuses on the Yangtze River Delta urban agglomeration in China as a case study. It bridges interpretable machine learning (XGBoost-SHAP) with structural causal modeling (SCM) to systematically quantify the nonlinear impacts and causal mechanisms of blue-green space (BGS) patterns and meteorological factors on land surface temperature (LST) and PM 2.5 concentrations. The results indicate that: (1) LST drivers exhibit a pronounced seasonal shift-BGS coverage dominates in summer, whereas meteorological factors prevail in winter-whereas PM 2.5 is consistently governed by wind speed across seasons; (2) key drivers exhibit threshold effects (e.g., in this study, 40-42% vegetation coverage for LST, 79-80% water aggregation for PM 2.5 ), beyond which they act as “effect-switching thresholds” that reverse the influence of other factors and form a nonlinear interaction network; and (3) SCM reveals the dual causal pathways through which BGS patterns influence the environment-via direct cooling and indirect modulation of wind fields-and quantitatively verifies the stable positive causal effect of PM 2.5 on LST, clarifying the pathway of “pollution exacerbating warming”. In summary, this study uncovers the nonlinear, threshold-dependent characteristics of the UHI-pollution complex system and elucidates their synergistic intensification from a causal perspective, providing a quantitative basis for seasonally adaptive strategies to synergistically mitigate urban heat and pollution.

title: Theory-informed and interpretable graph learning for urban commuting flows
Revealing land-use functional patterns and associated factors in China’s high-speed rail station areas: Based on self-organizing maps and explainable machine learning algorithms
abstract: The rapid expansion of high-speed rail (HSR) is closely associated with urban spatial restructuring. However, HSR station areas show substantial differentiation in land-use structure and functional positioning, and their functional patterns and associated characteristics remain insufficiently understood at the national scale. Taking 1570 HSR station areas in China as the research objects, this study constructs an integrated framework of comparative advantage, SOM clustering, and XGBoost-SHAP to identify land-use functional patterns in HSR station areas and analyze their associated factors. The results show that HSR station areas can be classified into four typical patterns: Public facility-dominated pattern (PFDP), Balanced multifunctional pattern (BMP), Industry-dominated pattern (IDP), and Commercial service-dominated pattern (CSDP). Their spatial distribution is closely related to regional industrial bases, city hierarchy, and the structure of the HSR network. The XGBoost-SHAP analysis further indicates that land-use diversity, bus accessibility, road network length, industrial structure, and distance to the city center are key variables closely associated with functional differentiation in station areas, and they show significant nonlinear responses and interaction-related characteristics in the model predictions for different functional patterns.This study contributes to a deeper understanding of functional differentiation in HSR station areas and provides theoretical support and planning guidance for HSR new town development, land use optimization, and urban functional restructuring.

title: From green space to park-based cooling potential: Performance-weighted walkable access to urban park cooling in Detroit
Urban green space percolation: From connectivity to ecological management mapping
abstract: Urban green spaces (UGS) are increasingly planned as connected networks, yet many connectivity assessments reduce cost variation to a static threshold and provide limited guidance on where to intervene. We develop a percolation-based framework for translating dynamic UGS connectivity into ecological management priorities. The framework constructs a least-cost, cost-weighted UGS network, activates edges in ascending cost-weighted distance to identify critical transitions and merger hierarchies, and converts the full percolation history into management zones, a three-level edge hierarchy, and a four-type node typology. Applied to Nanjing, China, the analysis shows that system-level connectivity emerges within a narrow high-cost critical band triggered by a small set of cross-barrier links. The merger history reveals three persistent spatial subsystems, which are further resolved into five management zones. Robustness experiments indicate that protecting map-prioritized edges and nodes slows the decline of weighted global efficiency under the tested removal rules. The framework links process-based connectivity diagnosis with spatially explicit planning actions, including corridor safeguarding, within-zone reinforcement, and stepping-stone protection, while remaining transferable with local calibration.

Urban airflow field prediction using sparse sensors: A hybrid data-driven approach with reduced-order modeling
abstract: Urban airflow field modeling can provide cities with monitoring solutions to enhance pedestrian/cyclists comfort, improve air quality, and enhance urban wind energy generation yield. In addition, it could support a safe and efficient deployment of urban air mobility (UAM) supporting the next generation of faster and more sustainable means of urban transport reducing the congestion and traffic. However, real-time wind monitoring across urban areas remains a significant challenge due to spatial and temporal variations and uncertainties. This study presents an integrated framework that serves as a surrogate model for the real-time reconstruction and prediction of wind velocity fields around a simplified urban building configuration. The approach relies exclusively on online sensor measurements and employs reduced-order modeling techniques for dimensionality reduction, thereby improving computational efficiency. The offline development of the model integrates three principal components: (1) a bidirectional long short-term memory (BILSTM) network trained on airflow sensor data to capture temporal dynamics, (2) a sparsity-promoting dynamic mode decomposition (SP-DMD) for extracting dominant spatial modes of airflow, and (3) a multi-task learning (MTL) network to map sensor signals. The proposed framework was assessed against high-fidelity CFD simulations of wind flow around a high-rise urban building. The results indicate that the proposed three-stage method reliably reconstructs accurate urban airflow fields in real time under varying levels of sensor noise, and demonstrate its feasibility for sparse-sensor reconstruction under the tested sensor-placement configurations. Moreover, these findings demonstrate that the proposed approach can significantly reduce operational/computational costs and shows strong potential as a surrogate tool for next-generation of urban airflow monitoring.

Walkable but not walkable? A mismatch between urban heat and pedestrian-oriented environments in promoting equitable climate resilience

Revealing the diurnal drivers of land surface temperature using artificial neural network models: A case study in Changsha-Zhuzhou-Xiangtan metropolitan area, China
Intermodal versus monomodal travellers: Evidence from a comparative study in Porto
abstract: Intermodality, i.e., the combination of more than one transport mode within a single trip, is increasingly being promoted as an alternative to car travel. However, empirical evidence on who adopts intermodal travel, how it differs from monomodal behaviour, and what motivates these choices in everyday contexts remains limited. The present study addresses this gap by systematically comparing intermodal and monomodal travellers in terms of sociodemographic characteristics, travel motivations, and observed travel behaviour through deploying a large-scale travel behaviour survey in the city of Porto, Portugal. The results reveal clear and consistent differences between intermodal and monomodal travellers. Intermodality is more prevalent among individuals aged over 23, those with higher education levels, and public transport pass holders, while monomodality is more common among younger travellers, retirees and larger households. Motivational factors play a central role: intermodality is strongly associated with public transport efficiency, higher service frequency, and the avoidance of car-related inconveniences such as congestion and parking difficulties. Safe and supportive walking and cycling infrastructure further facilitates intermodal travel by enabling effective first- and last-mile connections. At the trip level, intermodality is more likely for longer trips, commuting purposes, and trips involving bus, train or active modes. Overall, the findings highlight intermodality as a rational and context-dependent mobility strategy rather than a universal goal. The study offers policy-relevant insights for promoting intermodal travel through improved public transport performance, dedicated infrastructure for active modes, and reduced structural advantages for car-based travel.

Machine learning for urban wind simulation: A comprehensive review
abstract: Urban wind simulation plays an important role in pedestrian comfort assessment, wind safety evaluation, air quality analysis, and broader urban environmental planning. Conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) approaches, although physically grounded, remain computationally demanding and highly reliant on mesh quality, which makes them impractical for large-scale or iterative urban design workflows. This study reviews recent developments in data-driven, physics-informed, and hybrid machine learning methods for urban wind prediction, with attention to their modeling assumptions, validation strategies, and generalization behavior. The literature is organized along the urban wind simulation pipeline to provide a structured overview of current surrogate modeling approaches and their practical limitations. The review highlights open challenges related to robustness, benchmarking, and uncertainty quantification, and discusses directions for improving the reliability and scalability of ML-based urban wind modeling.

title: Crash-risk-aware routing for sustainable urban mobility: Balancing safety, efficiency, and energy under dynamic traffic conditions
Numerical simulation of the evolution of the temperature field of phase change temperature-regulating asphalt pavement under the urban heat island effect
Climate-specific and morphology-informed decarbonization policy for cities using urban building energy modeling
Evaluating vehicle-to-grid as a participation-dependent system flexibility resource: evidence from charging profiles and policy scenarios
abstract: Vehicle-to-grid (V2G) is increasingly discussed as a system flexibility resource, yet its system-level relevance depends less on technological capability than on whether electric vehicles can effectively participate under real-world institutional, behavioral, and operational conditions. This study examines pathways for system-relevant V2G deployment in South Korea by integrating a participation-oriented policy framework with a quantitative assessment of observed EV charging behavior. Using hourly EV charging electricity sales data for 2021–2023, this study constructs seasonal charging profiles and percentile-based charging peaks, and develops charging demand scenarios for 2030 and 2050. V2G potential is evaluated through an effective participation rate capturing five interdependent dimensions—user enrollment, plug-in availability, technical readiness, energy-related constraints, and operational feasibility—that shape realizable flexibility. Results show that accelerating EV diffusion intensifies evening charging peaks, increasing demand for peak-oriented system flexibility. Under these conditions, the scale and relevance of V2G are far more sensitive to effective participation than to the size of the underlying technical resource pool. Even modest participation can yield policy-relevant, gigawatt-scale V2G potential in the long term, whereas insufficient participation renders V2G systemically marginal regardless of technological capability. By conceptualizing participation as a multiplicative and policy-sensitive determinant of system outcomes, this study clarifies why many technically feasible V2G options remain unrealized in practice. The proposed framework links policy design, user behavior, and system impacts, providing a transferable basis for designing phased policy interventions that enable V2G to evolve from pilot applications to a system-level flexibility resource.

title: Deciphering the spatiotemporal dynamics and driving mechanisms of urban land green use efficiency in China: Insights from interpretable machine learning
Can green cycling paths reduce commuter exposure to ultrafine particles? A repeated measures study in Copenhagen, Denmark
abstract: ABSTRACT Background In urban environments, road traffic is the primary source of ultrafine particle (UFP) exposure. Cycling along green paths, away from traffic, may reduce commute-related air pollution exposure. This study quantifies commuter exposure to UFP in urban environments and the potential reduction when cycling on green paths. Methods Over six weeks (February-March 2024), 40 cycling trips were performed on a fixed 8.3 km route (∼35 minutes) in Copenhagen during rush-hour (07:45 h45h) and non-rush-hour (09:45 h). UFP in terms of particle number concentration (PNC) and geolocation were measured using a DiSCmini and GPS watch. We divided the route into the following segments: green cycling path, low traffic street, moderate traffic street, high traffic street. Generalized additive mixed models were used to compare average PNC levels across segments accounting for confounding factors such as meteorological factors and rush hours. Results Trip-mean PNC was ∼10,000 pt/cm 3 , ranging from ∼2200 to ∼25,000 pt/cm 3 . PNC varied substantially by location: highest levels were observed in high (mean (SD) of 11,460 (11,792) pt/cm 3 ) and moderate traffic (12,796 (10,433) pt/cm 3 ) segments and lowest levels along the green path (5,849 (5,380) pt/cm 3 ). After adjusting for confounders, cycling on the green path reduced by 32% to 50% PNC compared to higher-traffic segments (moderate traffic: rate ratio (RR) 0.68, 95% CI 0.62–0.76; high traffic RR 0.56 (95% CI 0.50, 0.62)). Conclusions Green cycling infrastructure can significantly reduce UFP exposure, supporting prioritizing investment in green cycling infrastructures as a public health intervention to protect active commuters in cities.

title: Designing sponge cities in data-scarce contexts: a machine learning–enabled land cover dynamics and urban hydrologic response framework for nature-based flood resilience
Unveiling scale effects of the built environment on urban innovation with explainable machine learning
Beyond single-element thresholds: Statistical compensatory effects among built environment factors in enhancing street vitality
Quantifying the impacts of urban form on air pollution using Local Climate Zone classifications in Greater London: a machine learning approach
abstract: Urban air pollution remains a persistent challenge for global cities. The Local Climate Zone (LCZ) framework, which classifies urban environments based on land cover, physical geometry, and thermal properties, has shown significant potential for air pollution research. However, few studies have quantitatively explored the relationship between air pollution and LCZs. To address this gap, the study combines ultra-high-resolution pollutant concentration data (PM 2.5 , PM 10 , NO 2 , NO x ; grid size 20m × 20m) with LCZs (grid size 100m × 100m) and applies interpretable machine learning models. The Extreme Gradient Boosting algorithm, combined with the SHapley Additive exPlanations is used. Findings from Greater London show that the trained machine learning model incorporating LCZ categories, spatial coordinates, and buffer features provides strong performance, with testing R² of 0.89 for PM 2.5 , 0.85 for PM 10 , 0.90 for NO 2 , and 0.82 for NO x . The most polluted LCZs (the three highest deviations above the overall average) are concentrated within only 3.82% of Greater London. These include LCZ1 (Compact highrise), LCZ2 (Compact midrise), LCZ10 (Heavy industry), and LCZE (Bare rock or paved surfaces), where maximum pollutant concentrations are up to 68% higher than the overall average. However, the LCZs ranked as having the strongest overall impact on air pollution do not always correspond to those with the highest pollution levels. Feature importance analysis shows that LCZ5 (open midrise) has a significant effect on air pollution in Greater London. This is partly due to dispersion of pollutants from highly polluted areas (particularly LCZ1, LCZ2 and LCZ10 in Inner London) towards Outer Greater London, combined with emissions within LCZ5, leading to a cumulative impact on overall pollution levels. Overall, the results show the LCZ framework, despite some limitations, is a valuable approach for quantifying air pollution research, providing insights not only into the spatial distribution of high-pollution areas but also into the key factors driving urban air pollution patterns.

title: Enhancing heatwave resilience in recreational public spaces: An operational tool from a Mediterranean Algerian urban context
abstract: Heatwaves are among the most pressing climate-related challenges for contemporary cities, threatening human health, social equity, and urban infrastructure. Recreational public spaces have significant potential to enhance heatwave resilience by providing thermal refuges, supporting urban greening, and enabling social and ecological functions. However, despite growing research on urban heat, these spaces remain underexplored from an operational resilience perspective, particularly due to a lack of operational indicators and reference values for concrete evaluation and targeted improvement. To address this gap, this study introduces HResRPS - Heat Resilient Recreational Public Spaces , an operational tool designed to evaluate and enhance heatwave resilience in these spaces. Developed within an Algerian Mediterranean context, using the city of Jijel as a revealing urban laboratory experiencing increasing heatwaves, the tool translates the cyclical nature of resilience by organizing it across three hierarchical levels: phases, attributes, and operational indicators. Deep learning-based semantic clustering supported the structuring of resilience attributes, while internal consensus and a multidisciplinary Delphi-AHP process reinforced the framework’s robustness. The final tool consists of three phases, eight attribute clusters, and 22 operational indicators supported by context-adapted reference values and a composite index. HResRPS enables the assessment of overall heatwave resilience in recreational public spaces, identifies specific strengths and weaknesses across phases and attributes, and guides targeted improvement actions according to specific indicators and relevant stakeholders. It also supports new urban design projects by serving as a checklist for integrating indicators into early design stages. Finally, it offers a practical approach to sustainable and heat-resilient urban development.

title: Exploring the cooling effects of park green spaces and their influencing factors from the perspective of urban-rural gradient
Designing urban networks for morphological resilience
abstract: This paper examines how neighborhood morphology shapes accessibility conditions that support neighborhood resilience in seven Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) cities. Rather than directly measuring resilience under disruption, this study focuses on how urban form and network design support efficient access to all destinations within the neighborhood under normal operating conditions, recognizing walking as the most reliable and safest mode when other transportation systems are constrained. Using a multi-radius Gravity analysis at 400 m and 800 m across 213 residential neighborhoods, this paper evaluates the precondition for neighborhood resilience of urban form under three categories: highly resilient, moderately resilient, and fragile. The findings indicate that the built landscapes of organically developed Arab cities, as well as early Western planning models, demonstrate higher levels of resilience compared to contemporary urban forms characterized by auto-centricity and large-scale development patterns. Public-sector developments generally outperform private-sector projects in terms of resilience. However, several compact private typologies perform comparably to the strongest public examples, demonstrating that resilient urban morphologies are achievable under both planning regimes. These findings raise important questions about the prevailing capitalist approaches to private urban development in the region. The morphological attributes most strongly associated with resilience and high accessibility include plot density, intersection density, and street network configuration. As resilience has not yet been systematically translated into urban design codes and regulatory frameworks, this research provides strong empirical evidence and establishes a foundation for shaping more resilient urban forms in the GCC and beyond.

title: Land-Climate-Heating Nexus: Framework for institutional heating characterization and prediction
A two-stage optimization framework for improving outdoor thermal comfort in residential block designs

Wind and thermal comfort performance of the fourth-generation apartment housing in Northern and Southern China based on the “CFD–APMV” method
A causal deep learning framework for simulating the thermal impact of urban land use changes
abstract: As cities face increasingly warmer conditions, exacerbated by rapid urbanization and climate change, planners lack scalable tools to predict the thermal outcomes of specific landscape interventions. This research presents a causal deep learning framework that moves beyond thermal association to simulate the counterfactual thermal impacts of urban land-use changes. Using Detroit, Michigan, as a case study, a U-Net Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was developed to estimate Land Surface Temperature (LST) by integrating 2D spatial proxies, including multi-spectral indices, albedo, and building density. The model’s performance is validated through a series of “natural experiments” using a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) logic, comparing simulated impacts with real-world land-use transitions observed between 2019 and 2025. Results indicate high predictive fidelity ( R2 of 0.95 ± 0.005, Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.404 ± 0.030 K, Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.509 ± 0.025 K) and nearly 100% accuracy in predicting the direction of thermal change across all test cases. Physical interpretability analyses via Integrated Gradients confirmed the framework learned plausible, non-linear relationships, such as cooling thresholds for vegetation and the structural shading effects of high-density urban canyons. While the model successfully isolates landscape-driven thermal signals, it exhibits a conservative bias, especially in industrial areas where anthropogenic heat is a dominant factor. This framework offers a globally scalable, data-efficient solution for cities to improve sustainability and resiliency in the face of a changing climate, providing a robust evidence base for “what-if” urban planning scenarios and proactive climate equity research.

title: Towards a dynamic assessment of heat stress in indoor and near-outdoor urban environments
Innovation network embeddedness and urban system resilience in China: Spatial associations and structural differences
