Assessing the spatial distribution pattern of urban green space and its association with the hypertension prevalence rate in Beijing: A study in perspective of health benefits
abstract: ABSTRACT Urban green space (UGS) is an important component of urban landscape, the core of sustainable, ecological, livable and safe urban environment, and a key infrastructure supporting human health and well-being. Although its health benefits have been widely recognized, little is known about the relationship between the spatial distribution pattern of green spaces and health, especially in densely populated central urban areas. This study focuses on the central urban area of Beijing, relying on large health sample data, combined with green space information obtained from the GEE cloud platform, as well as data on air quality and socio-economic dynamics. Through statistical analysis, it reveals how the urban greenspace spatial pattern (UGSP) affects the hypertension prevalence rate (HPR). Research has shown that the morphology, spatial relationships, and spatial configurations of UGS exhibit significant imbalances, and there is a significant correlation and spatial correspondence between UGSP, HPR, and air quality. UGSP mainly indirectly affects residents' health through the mediating effect of air quality (CO), among which PLAND, AI, MPS, LPI, COHESION, and MSI play important roles. After integrating the above indicators, there are significant differences in HPR between sub-districts of different green space pattern categories. Therefore, based on the principle of equitable distribution, priority should be given to optimizing key pattern indicators in areas with weak green resource foundations. These findings and conclusions contribute to an understanding of the fairness of UGSP and will also guide future design and planning of UGS based on environmental health benefits.

title: Artificial intelligence policy and urban resilience: Evidence from a Quasi-natural experiment in China
Navigating the accuracy-efficiency trade-off in urban building energy modelling: A systematic review
Digital infrastructure construction and urban green transition: A quasi-natural experiment based on the broadband China policy using double machine learning
Impact of natural and artificial cover on LST in cities, with a focus on comparison of single- and multi-ring buffers
abstract: Land surface temperature (LST) is a representative indicator for predicting urban heat island. The single-buffer approach, which has been used to analyze the relationship between LST and explanatory variables, cannot capture the effects of both the distance of independent variables and the area of land cover included within the buffer zone. Therefore, we aimed to investigate the relationship between LST and natural and artificial land cover in urban regions, using a multi-ring buffer model to refine independent variables in 50-m increments, by land cover type. Four tree-based machine learning models—Random Forest, LightGBM, CatBoost, and XGBoost—were compared. XGBoost exhibited the highest performance, with R² range of 0.88–0.98 across 50–500-m intervals. LST prediction analysis was effective up to 350 m. Further, the significant spatial range of variables shifted with 50-m intervals, enabling a more granular analysis of the significant spatial range of independent variables. The restoration simulation showed that greening efforts on the Western Arterial Road and Jemulpo Tunnel reduced LST within an approximate range of 150 m. These findings provide crucial scientific evidence for determining the placement of urban parks and formulating urban planning and management strategies aimed at optimizing LST reduction in urban environments.

title: Influence of 2D/3D urban landscape on land surface temperature from the perspective of urban functional zones
Navigating uncertainty: An adaptive framework for resilient recovery of coupled infrastructure under stochastic disaster impacts
Bridging objective and subjective heat stress: A human-centered multiscale review of urban thermal experience
abstract: Urban heat stress research has rapidly advanced in measuring and modeling thermal exposure, yet a persistent gap remains between objective heat stress (OHS) and subjective heat stress (SHS). Existing reviews often examine these streams separately and lack a unified human-centered perspective for explaining their divergence. This study conducts a PRISMA-guided systematic review of 223 studies, including OHS-focused studies (n = 68), SHS-focused studies (n = 56), and conceptual or mechanistic studies that support the analysis of OHS–SHS relationships and underlying mismatch mechanisms (n = 99). The results reveal clear structural differences between the OHS- and SHS-focused research streams. OHS studies generally rely on environmental variables and thermal indices, forming relatively consistent methodological pathways across city, street, and person-based exposure levels. In contrast, SHS studies are more heterogeneous and context-dependent, with data sources ranging from individual-level surveys and interviews to participatory sensing, thermal walks, and large-scale digital traces such as social media. The review further identifies three recurrent sources of OHS–SHS mismatch: (1) differences in observation units, (2) scale-dependent representations of heat processes, and (3) limited integration of physiological processes linking environmental conditions to perceived experience. Building on these findings, we propose a human-centered integrated framework that conceptualizes heat experience as a process linking environmental exposure, physiological response, and perceptual–expressive outcomes, with behavior acting as a key modulator. This framework provides a conceptual basis for multi-source integration, cross-scale validation, and discrepancy-based heat-risk assessment, supporting a shift toward more experience-oriented urban heat governance.

title: From risk intensity to risk inequality: Unraveling the spatial inequality and drivers of urban heat health risk in high-density cities
Density or diversity? Untangling the roles of points of interest (POIs) in shaping urban vitality
abstract: Urban vitality is a fundamental indicator of sustainable urban development, yet the distinct roles of land use density and diversity remain insufficiently understood. This study examines how these factors influence urban vitality across different neighborhood contexts in Shenzhen, using mobile signaling data as a proxy for vitality. We operationalize neighborhood context through indicators of road density, floor area ratio (FAR), and point-of-interest (POI) characteristics, and classify urban areas into three types: high context with low vitality (HL), low context with high vitality (LH), and balanced areas. Our findings demonstrate that form-function and vitality partitioning outperforms approaches relying solely on form and vitality. XGBoost models are then employed to examine how POI density, POI diversity, and specific POI categories contribute to vitality in each context. The results show that in HL areas, POI density positively influences vitality, whereas further diversification at lower levels yields diminishing returns. Furthermore, in LH areas, increasing POI density exerts a stronger positive effect on vitality than diversity. Additionally, the density of shopping, accommodation service, and sports & recreation enhances vitality in HL areas, while the density of transportation service and science/culture & education service boosts it in LH areas. These findings emphasize the importance of context-sensitive land use strategies: prioritizing core functions to revitalize areas where the context is strong but vitality is lacking, and applying specific renewal measures to optimize capacity where vitality thrives despite a weaker context.

title: Physics-informed sensor placement for street canyon wind field reconstruction
A causal network for strategic foresight of inclusive climate actions through co-creation of nature-based solutions
abstract: Urban systems exhibit complex dynamics that create interrelated environmental, social, and economic challenges. While most studies focus on sector-specific issues, recent approaches address urban complexity through comprehensive frameworks grounded on Systems thinking. In this context, Inclusive Climate Actions (ICAs) are adopted not only to mitigate and adapt to climate change, but also to deliver social and economic benefits. Nevertheless, the impacts of ICAs within urban systems remain largely unexplored. This study develops a digital decision-support tool based on a foresight methodology to facilitate the co-creation of urban development scenarios through ICAs , such as Nature-based Solutions, integrated within complex urban systems. The methodology constructs a causal network that defines the relationships between ICAs and pre-defined Key Performance Indicators, and operationalizes it as digital decision-support tool. Additionally, the network defines interrelationships among KPIs, highlighting synergies and trade-offs. The tool estimates the relative changes induced by the actions selected by users, both numerically and spatially. The digital decision-support tool is designed to automate the estimation process, and can be used during participatory workshops with local stakeholders, citizens, and public administrations to provide real-time information on the impacts of selected actions. This work is part of the DUT-funded GREEN-INC project.

title: Assessing bicycle convenience in car-dependent cities
abstract: To address issues associated with traditional motorised transport, urban mobility is undergoing a profound transformation. Although cycling is being promoted as an alternative to the car in the mobility plans of several Mediterranean cities, the proportion of people using it remains low. While establishing adequate infrastructure and services is necessary, it is not sufficient to encourage behavioural change. Alongside physical interventions, soft measures are also required. Intuitive tools that compare the costs (not limited to monetary ones) of different transport modes with cycling are necessary. Such tools have been developed for other fields or modes but are currently lacking for bicycles. To address this gap, this study presents a methodology for developing a useroriented decision-support tool that evaluates the economic, spatial and environmental effects of switching from motorised to bicycle transport in car-dependent cities. It assesses several key performance indicators derived from a review of the scientific literature. These include health impacts, congestion rates, connectivity and the user-friendliness and security of the relevant infrastructure. Different user profiles enable a tailored evaluation for each respondent. The architecture of the tool is presented and the prototype is then tested through a targeted pilot distribution in the Metropolitan City of Venice (Italy). The results should be interpreted as a proof of concept rather than as representative estimates of population-level cycling potential. They illustrate each respondent's performance according to their identified journey, providing a more informed understanding of their choices. Furthermore, some of the answers relating to the criticalities of the network can be translated into data-driven recommendations for urban and transport planners. This suggests that, to improve the potential of bicycles as a sustainable transport mode in car-dependent urban areas, physical interventions related to modal choice should be complemented by behavioural initiatives.

title: Corrigendum to “Scale-dependent contributions of local and neighborhood influences on LCZ thermal variation” [Sustainable Cities and Society 148 (2026) 107621]
Compound daytime-nighttime high-temperature risk assessment: Heat event duration across 2050 counties and districts in China
Comparative assessment of heat mitigation strategies across hotspot local climate zones in a hot arid city
abstract: Urban heat stress in cities has intensified due to rapid urbanization (land use/land cover changes), which led to higher urban temperatures, substantially worsened outdoor thermal comfort (OTC), and increased building energy demand. Although investigations of urban heat mitigation strategies are extensive, they are not systematic or comprehensive, limiting the comparability between findings. Therefore, this study presents an integrated, transferable framework that links high-resolution local climate zone (LCZ) classification, long-term thermal hotspot identification, microclimate simulation, and building energy assessment to evaluate urban heat mitigation strategies. Using Doha as a case study, the city was classified into built (LCZs 1–6) and land cover (LCZs A–F) classes through a high-resolution LiDAR-GIS approach (overall accuracy: 95.7%), revealing substantial discrepancies relative to the global 100 m LCZ product. Analysis of Landsat imagery showed that compact urban forms are thermal hotspots, with mean summer land surface temperature reaching 43°C in compact midrise areas (LCZ 2) and 42°C in compact low-rise areas (LCZ 3). Two representative hotspot study areas (Mansoura-LCZ 2 and Salwa-LCZ 3) were selected, and their microclimates were simulated using the ENVI-met model for typical midsummer days. The model performance was evaluated against on-site measurements. Baseline simulations show severe urban thermal stress (T a > 40°C, MRT > 70°C, PET > 54°C for much of daytime). Eight mitigation scenarios based on green infrastructure and cool materials are comparatively evaluated. Green infrastructure scenarios provided consistent OTC benefits, with tree canopies producing the greatest localized cooling (T a reductions of 3–5°C, MRT reductions >15°C). Building energy simulations for July show the largest cooling demand reductions for building envelope interventions (15–25%), while tree cover scenarios produced limited savings (<3%). Overall, the study implements a cross-scale methodology for evaluating heat mitigation strategies while revealing key trade-offs in their impacts on T a , OTC, and building energy performance.

title: Systemic resilience of the urban educational facility system: A spatiotemporal framework coupling chronic stresses and acute shocks
abstract: Amidst the interactive effects of demographic structural contraction and frequent natural hazards, the resilience goals of the educational facility system face a critical trade-off between long-term operational efficiency and emergency functional robustness. Previous studies have frequently examined school consolidation or disaster reinforcement in isolation, neglecting the spatiotemporal coupling effects between long-term adaptability and instantaneous robustness. To address this gap, this study draws on Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS) theory to construct a three-dimensional assessment framework evaluating the inherent resilience, adaptability, and robustness of educational facilities. Using Kumamoto City, Japan, as an empirical case, this study quantified the comprehensive performance of the facility system under long-term demographic changes (2020–2070) and multi-hazard scenarios (earthquakes and floods), and identified five typical resilience patterns using K-means clustering. The results indicate that the resilience patterns of educational facilities exhibit significant structural and spatial differentiation characteristics: facilities in the central built-up core face risks of future resource obsolescence due to socio-spatial mismatch, while those in peripheral areas are highly susceptible to functional overload when accommodating transferred evacuation demands during acute shocks. Spatial analysis shows that the distribution of such resilience risks is not homogeneous; rather, it exhibits localized agglomeration that closely aligns with micro-natural geomorphology and demographic evolution patterns. The assessment framework and typology-based intervention strategies developed in this study provide quantitative support for formulating differentiated disaster mitigation strategies and resource integration schemes for public service facilities in shrinking cities.

title: Quantifying the effect of psychological adaptation: A new model for outdoor thermal comfort evaluation in urban public spaces — A case study in the hot-summer and cold-winter zone
Monetizing diurnal thermal inequity: Spatial-economic valuation and spatially targeted adaptation under jobs-housing separation
Quantifying expressway traffic resilience to freezing rain: An empirical and spatial analysis using ETC data
Topographic conditioning of urban–rural gradients in surface urban heat island intensity across climatic contexts: Evidence from 341 Chinese cities
Evaluation of cold islands mitigation benefits in heat island city based on connectivity
Mortality risks of co-exposure to extreme heat and ozone in urban populations: Synergy, vulnerability, and implications for public health
Mapping urban environmental stress in Barcelona: a multivariate approach using GWPCA
abstract: This study develops a spatially explicit Environmental Stress Index (ESI) for Barcelona, integrating six key environmental dimensions (air pollution, noise, thermal stress, population density, park accessibility, and green cover) across 1,068 census tracts. Using Geographically Weighted Principal Component Analysis, the analysis captures local spatial heterogeneity in environmental stress and derives location-specific weights to construct a multidimensional composite indicator. The ESI synthesises multivariate data into a spatially explicit diagnostic tool, identifying intraurban disparities and dominant stressors at the local level. Results reveal that 45% of the population is exposed to above-average environmental stress, particularly in central, eastern, and northern areas, despite these zones covering only 25% of the city’s area. By using a localised multivariate analysis, the framework offers a policy relevant diagnostic tool that enables the detection of high-stress areas driven by environmental inequalities, supporting the effective targeting of interventions at the intraurban scale. Its scalability and adaptability make it suitable for application in other urban contexts, supporting data-driven strategies for urban sustainability, climate adaptation, and environmental justice.

title: Urban morphology as a driver of urban sustainability trade-offs and synergies: an explainable graph neural network analysis of Singapore

Corrigendum to “Collaboratively optimize of multi-scale spatial form within urban blocks for low-carbon performance: A machine learning-driven design support framework” [Sustainable Cities and Society, 143 (2026), 107342]
Beyond greener, bluer, and more accessible: Rethinking urban public space design for restorativeness and Informal Social Interaction
Strategic and equitable allocation of electric vehicle fast charging stations using geospatial-aware multi-objective deep reinforcement learning
Spatial mismatch and association network of urban flood risk and resilience from a supply–demand perspective: A case study of Beijing, China
Control strategies in fifth-generation district heating and cooling systems: A review
abstract: The sustained increase in global energy demand, coupled with the urgent pursuit of sustainable cities and districts, is accelerating the transformation of thermal energy systems. District heating and cooling networks provide an efficient pathway for integrating renewable energy, waste heat, and thermal energy storage in areas with high thermal demand density. Among these systems, fifth-generation district heating and cooling (5GDHC) systems have attracted increasing attention because they operate at near-ambient temperature levels and enable bidirectional heating and cooling exchange among decentralized prosumers through local heat pumps. These characteristics make 5GDHC systems a promising pathway for low-carbon thermal energy supply, but they also introduce new operational control challenges related to dynamic network interactions, flexible demand, and coordinated energy exchange. However, existing research on 5GDHC systems mainly focuses on system design and planning, while relatively limited attention has been given to operational control strategies and control methods. This gap restricts the practical deployment of 5GDHC systems. This study presents a systematic and critical review of recent advances in 5GDHC operational control. It analyses existing control objectives and methodological frameworks and discusses the key limitations of current control strategies as well as the challenges and future directions for practical implementation.

title: Spatial gradient characteristics of local heat island effects in urban villages embedded in different environments
Prioritizing jogging-friendly streets in active mobility planning: A decision-support framework integrating trajectory evidence and expert judgment

From physical surfaces to human-centric heat stress: LST and UTCI heat mapping reveals nonlinear effects of urban morphology
abstract: Heat exposure connects the built environment and public health, directly shaping the livability and sustainability of urban areas. Fully understanding the spatial heterogeneity of heat exposure and its driving factors is therefore a vital prerequisite for climate-adaptive urban planning. However, most planning-oriented studies rely on land surface temperature (LST), and whether LST adequately represents human heat exposure and how it differs from physiologically relevant heat stress remains insufficiently examined. Here, adopting Landsat-retrieved 30-m LST and GPU-accelerated 1-m universal thermal climate index (UTCI) in Singapore, this study establishes a comprehensive “Modeling-Comparing-Assessing” framework to systematically evaluate the spatial and mechanistic discrepancies between the two metrics. We further investigate pronounced non-stationary and threshold-based quantitative relationships of the two metrics with urban factors by employing a novel geographically weighted XGBoost (GW-XGBoost) and generalized additive model (GAM) workflow. Our results demonstrate notable discrepancies in spatial patterns of LST and UTCI, along with substantial spatial heterogeneity in how 2D and 3D urban factors impact these two thermal metrics, as revealed by explainable GW-XGBoost models (the test R 2 = 0.855 for LST and 0.905 for UTCI, respectively). Crucially, spatially explicit SHAP interprets that sky view factor plays a central role in explaining UTCI variability but exhibits a comparatively marginal independent contribution to LST, indicating that LST inadequately captures shading-driven and radiative processes governing actual human heat stress. Notably, SHAP-GAM analysis indicates that higher albedo is associated with increased UTCI. These novel findings provide model-informed planning implications for integrating physiologically relevant thermal indices to support targeted heat risk management and climate-adaptive urban planning.

Fine-scale carbon emission assessment for low-carbon transition in national-level new areas: Exploring driving mechanisms of industrial layout, socioeconomic factors, and ecological environment
Development and optimal sizing of an integrated renewable energy system for sustainable cities
abstract: This study presents an integrated energy system aimed at promoting and supporting sustainable cities and communities through techno-economic and environmental optimization. The system is modeled using the REopt optimization tool developed by NREL and represents a multi-building campus comprising a large office, warehouse, primary school, supermarket, and a mid-rise residential building. The proposed scenario integrates photovoltaic (PV) systems, wind energy, battery energy storage (BES), chilled water thermal energy storage (TES), and grid interaction. The optimization framework evaluates system performance from energy, economic, and environmental perspectives in line with the source–system–service (3S) approach. The obtained results indicate that the optimized scenario reduces peak grid demand by approximately 30–35% through effective load shifting by energy storage and renewable energy integration. In the optimized scenario, the annual electricity demand of nearly 13 GWh is primarily supplied by the grid (67.3%), followed by PV generation (25.3%), battery discharge (7%), and wind energy. The battery system reaches a round-trip efficiency of 90.2%. The system prioritizes energy storage-based operation, reduces reliance on real-time electricity generation, and lowers operational costs. Environmental analysis reveals substantial emission reductions, including approximately 11,533 tonnes of CO 2 -eq, along with significant reductions in NO x , SO 2 , and PM2.5 throughout the system's life cycle. The overall system energy efficiency is found to be 23.57% on a source-to-service basis under the specified energy mix, with renewable energy and energy storage integration. The proposed system also supports urban decarbonization by reducing grid dependency and alleviating pressure on the existing electricity infrastructure.

title: A standardised Digital Twin design framework for transport system decarbonisation
abstract: Decarbonising transport systems is a global necessity for achieving net-zero, and Digital Twin (DT) technologies are emerging as key enablers of this transition. Despite growing interest in DT solutions, their potential support for transport decarbonisation remains in its infancy. This is mainly due to inconsistent methodological development and limited alignment with established standards. The literature shows that IoT, CPS, and embedded systems are increasingly used in DT design across the transport modes. However, they often target fragmented and function-specific use cases rather than integrated, system-level applications. This paper fills these gaps by presenting a novel Digital Twin Design Framework for transport system decarbonisation that, to the authors’ knowledge, is the first to adapt the ISO-23247 manufacturing standard to the transport domain. The study combines a systematic literature review of more than 100 studies with a Delphi consultation involving 10 experts from three UK research institutions using more than 10,000 extracted literature and workshop-derived data records. The analysis identifies (1) dominant digital methodologies used in transport DT development, and (2) standardised architectural elements essential for a unified DT design for transport decarbonisation across road, rail, marine/maritime and air. The proposed framework encompasses a layered architecture comprising observable, communication, control, user, and cross-system DT entities. The proposed framework provides a scalable reference architecture for supporting interoperable, climate-aligned DT development across transport systems. It also offers a blueprint for aligning transport digitalisation with climate policy and net-zero objectives.

title: Seasonal responses of the thermal environment to landscape pattern and land use/land cover under multiple drivers in the Beijing–Tianjin–Hebei urban agglomeration, China
AutoBEM: A scalable framework for nationwide building energy simulation and retrofit evaluation in the United States
Equity in motion: Assessing metro–micromobility accessibility and spatial heterogeneity through trip-chain analysis in Zhengzhou, China
abstract: Metro systems are widely evaluated as engines of urban accessibility, yet equity inferences often rely on station- or in-vehicle–centric measures that omit substantial door-to-door frictions. This study develops a trip-chain, multimodal metro accessibility framework for Zhengzhou, China, explicitly modelling access/egress travel, in-station circulation, waiting, and rail travel across nine feasible chain configurations combining walking, cycling, and e-bike connections. We identified five employment clusters using job-capacity–weighted firm density, and evaluated the modelled potential time-accessibility for 6,119 housing compounds, distinguishing commercial, public, and resettlement housing as proxies for social differentiation. Results show that incorporating trip-chain segments yields materially different inferred accessibility and equity patterns relative to core-only representations and reveals socially patterned mismeasurement under a 2SFCA benchmark, with the largest overestimation and dispersion concentrated in peripheral belts and among social-housing compounds. Micromobility feasibility compresses mean accessibility gaps between housing groups by reducing feeder-time penalties, but these gains are uneven across space and remain configuration-dependent. To capture this dimension, we introduce a Mode-Sensitivity Index (MSI) that quantifies configurational stability as cross-chain variability in door-to-door travel time. MSI is systematically higher for public and resettlement housing and exhibits a U-shaped belt profile, indicating greater chain dependence in both major-node and outer-belt contexts. The findings suggest that equitable metro planning requires evaluating not only average accessibility but also the robustness of access across plausible door-to-door chains. The proposed framework and MSI provide transferable diagnostics for metro-oriented cities integrating rail expansion, social housing, and shared micromobility.

title: Quantifying the impact of heatwaves on urban nighttime economic activities using daily nighttime lights data in China

Where could urban tree canopy expansion lower modeled summer cooling-energy demand? An equity-informed explainable machine-learning framework for Washington, DC
Unraveling spatial heterogeneity and nonlinearity: A dual-method analysis of the impacts of built environment factors on ride-hailing demand
Directional mean radiant temperature decomposition reveals micro-scale drivers of urban heat stress in Novi Sad (Serbia)
abstract: Urban heat stress is an increasing issue with large implications for health and comfort. This study investigates micro-scale drivers of heat stress in Novi Sad, Serbia, using mobile meteorological carts to obtain measurements at 29 locations with diverse urban design during a hot, cloud-free summer day. Air temperature, relative humidity, wind speed and six-directional short- and longwave radiation were recorded and used to compute Mean Radiant Temperature (MRT) and Physiological Equivalent Temperature (PET). PET values ranged from 25°C to 56°C, indicating slight to extreme heat stress. Sensitivity analysis showed MRT as the dominant driver of spatial differences in PET during daytime. Decomposition of radiant load revealed that longwave lateral radiation contributed most to radiant load, but lateral shortwave contributions were most variable, because of the variability in local shading. Sky View Factor (SVF) appeared a strong predictor of MRT and PET, with a 10 % reduction in SVF lowering MRT up to 5°C. In contrast, surface type (grass vs. impervious) had only minor effects, limited to reduced upward longwave radiation in the afternoon and evening. Buildings and trees achieved comparable maximum MRT reductions, though tree-induced shading exhibited greater variability. These results show the importance of directional radiant load decomposition for identifying which radiative pathways contribute most to heat stress and when. By distinguishing the dominant solar and longwave components—and their dependence on SVF, shading type, and surface materials—this approach provides site-specific empirical evidence on the radiative mechanisms that shaped pedestrian heat stress under clear-sky, low-wind conditions in a temperate climate city.

title: Corrigendum to “Water-Land-Energy-Carbon nexus in cities: A dynamic model with evidence from Beijing” [Sustainable Cities and Society 148 (2026) 107579]
Role of life and exogeneous events on habit disruptions affecting public bike sharing choices
abstract: Public Bike Sharing System (PBSS) choices can be influenced by events that disrupt established habits, with triggers arising from personal life changes or external events. This paper discusses the impacts of life and exogeneous events on habit disruptions that affect travel choices in the context of PBSS, particularly on modal shift from and to shared bicycle systems. We employed mixed logit models based on calendar-format survey data obtained from public bike sharing users to explore the connection between several life and exogenous events, individual sociodemographic factors, and the decisions to start or stop using a public bike-sharing system. Exogeneous events have been considered into the models as a single variable because of data availability constraints. A case study in São Paulo, Brazil, showed that relocating farther from work or school, obtaining a college degree, starting remote study or a new job, and accounting for exogenous events impact the shift towards PBSS. In turn, working remotely and exogenous events impact the shift from PBSS to other transport modes. Therefore, policymaking to foster shared bicycle use should promote station visibility and interventions such as the development of cycling lanes and speed reduction measures to ensure that the benefits of PBSS support sustainable mobility. New pricing strategies that prioritize convenience can also contribute to diversifying the user profile of shared bicycles. Also, considering shared bicycles systems as part of public transport rather than solely focusing on the balance between costs and revenues would benefit the population, thus fostering a more sustainable urban mobility system.

title: Uncovering the endogenous dynamics of intercity population mobility: Evidence from urban networks in China
A co-production approach to identify and visualise vulnerability to urban extreme heat in Nottingham, UK
abstract: Adapting cities to extreme heat is a key global challenge that is exacerbated by the increasing frequency and severity of heatwaves. Critical to developing robust adaptation strategies is understanding where the greatest risk of negative impacts are located and why communities are vulnerable, i.e. unpicking the complex interrelationships between physiological factors, economic deprivation, and environmental constraints. This study presents a co-production approach to develop the first heat vulnerability index (HVI) for Nottingham, UK, a city with strong climate adaptation aspirations, to provide evidence for informing local policy-making regarding where to target adaptation strategies to reduce heat vulnerabilities. The HVI was co-produced with the Blue-Green Nottingham Group (BGNG) that aims to unite scientific and practice-based knowledge and align academic research with current policy development. This represents an advancement from traditional HVIs developed without stakeholder input. We identify and interpret the spatial distribution of vulnerability (comprising exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity) to extreme heat and highlight locations at greatest risk. This includes communities with high heat exposure determined by land surface temperature (e.g. due to limited urban green infrastructure (UGI) and dense urban development) and high sensitivity to heat that is driven by high unemployment, disability and vulnerable age groups (e.g. young children). The cooling potential of UGI and urban trees is shown to be important for enhancing adaptive capacity. Our study also demonstrates the value of novel geospatial visualisation technologies (e.g. Projection Augmented Relief Models; PARMs) in co-producing HVIs and for enhancing stakeholder engagement with climate risk and adaptation datasets.

title: Diagnosing low carbon practice performance across 297 Chinese cities: A dimension-process dual perspective assessment
abstract: Urban China is the key contributor to the country’s carbon emissions, making the assessment on the urban low carbon practices essential for achieving carbon reduction targets. This study evaluates 297 prefecture-level-and-above Chinese cities using dimension-process dual perspectives diagnosis model that examines urban low carbon performance across eight performance dimensions (e.g. energy structure, economic development) and five management process activities (plan, implementation, check, outcome, and feedback). Results show significant variation in low carbon performance among Chinese cities, influenced by economic, geographic, and management culture differences. While dimensions such as economic development show comparatively better results, overall urban low-carbon performance in China is suboptimal and uneven. Significant weaknesses in ‘check’ and ‘feedback’ processes across most dimensions severely impede the establishment of an adaptive low carbon management culture. The study underscores that enhancing the evaluation and feedback mechanisms within the management cycle is crucial for improving overall urban low-carbon practice effectiveness and achieving sustainable urban transitions in China. The findings provide city administrators with a diagnostic tool for identifying specific process weaknesses and prioritizing targeted interventions, and offer policymakers a replicable framework for monitoring nationwide progress towards carbon neutrality.

title: Spatiotemporal quantification of electric vehicle charging carbon footprint for urban governance
Whose future? Citizens shaping green–blue infrastructure scenarios in European cities – a review and proposed framework
abstract: Cities are epicentres of climate change, threatening the liveability, resilience and equity of urban communities, requiring rapid and, in some cases, radical grey to green (and blue) transitions. Green-blue infrastructure responds to these challenges by delivering multifunctional and strategically planned benefits from nature within cities. Yet, planning largely remains technocratic, limiting citizen agency. While participatory scenario planning is an established method to co-develop and envision resilient urban futures in cities, the extent of citizen involvement remains unclear. This paper makes two contributions, first it synthesises the evidence on how citizen insights and citizen-generated data are incorporated into green-blue infrastructure scenario planning across Europe, revealing key patterns and gaps in participation. Second it introduces the novel Citizen Scenario Cycle, a conceptual framework for analysing and strengthening citizen participation and citizen agency across the scenario planning process. Following PRISMA guidelines, a systematic identified thirty-six eligible publications from searches of academic and grey literature. Data was extracted that classified scenario characteristics, methodological approaches, participation modes and insights from citizen inclusion. The results reveal citizen participation is unevenly distributed amongst scenario stages, often concentrated to design/validation stages, and performing contributory roles, rather than substantive and sustained co-creation. Diverse and vulnerable communities were also poorly represented, as was clear evidence of policy uptake. Despite growing emphasis on participatory futures, and evidence of methodological plurality, epistemic authority to citizens is limited and the governance conditions shaping citizen influence remain poorly understood. We conclude with targeted recommendations to further respond to the challenges and gaps identified.

title: How severe is sunlight deprivation in urban residential communities? A perspective from architectural and vegetation shading
Revealing urban resilience under flood stress: A dynamic assessment approach based on normal cloud score
Environmental assessment of housing and mobility: A review of studies on residential location effects
abstract: This review synthesizes the findings of 65 studies to examine the environmental footprint of residential locations, emphasizing the importance of integrating housing and transport dimensions, as well as distinguishing between direct and indirect impacts. The results show that housing typically accounts for 56% of the total residential footprint, with emissions ranging from 0.82 to 7.50 tCO₂eq/capita-year, while transport contributes 0.20 to 4.70 tCO₂eq/capita-year. In suburban areas, transport can surpass housing as the dominant contributor. Notably, indirect mobility impacts—such as vehicle manufacturing, infrastructure, and fuel production—are often underestimated, despite averaging 47% of total transport-related emissions. Key influencing factors include residential location (proximity to urban centers, density, transit access), housing type and size, and household socioeconomic characteristics. Sensitivity analyses indicate that promoting public transit and active travel modes, increasing urban density, and diversifying housing stock can significantly reduce emissions. However, strategies such as EV adoption or housing retrofits, while effective, require substantial investment and offer modest cost savings. The review also identifies persistent methodological and data-related limitations. Many studies rely on simplified representations of household mobility or use aggregated data, leading to inaccuracies and limiting the identification of household-scale emission hotspots. The rare inclusions of economic indicators also indicate a potential area for further research, as economic and social dimensions remain essential to a full understanding of sustainable housing and mobility systems.

title: Same urban form, differentiated heat outcomes: Climate sensitive thresholds of thermal environment and cross-climate transferability across eight U.S. metropolitan areas
How the built environment promotes sustainable commuting mode choice among groups with heterogeneous travel preferences?
Trade-off and synergy relationships in grey-green infrastructure influence regional inequality in extreme rainfall-flood resilience across 15 urban agglomerations in China
Modeling three-dimensional built-up volume dynamics and projections using long-term satellite observations
How fine is fine enough? - Impacts of temperature data resolution on heat-aware pedestrian routing
Stable decisions in unstable climates: Designing robust adaptive pathways for transition to a circular water economy in water-stressed cities
Quantifying the thermal mitigation effects of urban parks under different irrigation scenarios and tree-densities using ENVI-met and field measurements
Indoor–outdoor heat stress, housing characteristics, and health outcomes in an informal settlement: a mixed‑methods study from Dar es Salaam, Tanzania
abstract: Informal settlement residents in the Global South are often at high risk of extreme heat, not only because of elevated exposure but also because of low adaptive capacity and socio-environmental vulnerability, including substandard housing and limited access to cooling. However, measured evidence on how indoor–outdoor heat exposure, housing conditions, thermal perception, and self-reported health outcomes are related remains limited. This study examined these relationships in an informal settlement in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania, using a mixed-methods approach that combined indoor and outdoor microclimate monitoring, household surveys, housing characterization, and regression analysis. Outdoor daytime temperatures frequently exceeded 35°C, with Heat Index values often reaching “danger” levels; 70% of monitored days included conditions within the “danger” category. Nighttime heat exposure also remained elevated, particularly in February and March. At the community level, survey responses provided contextual support for the monitored indoor heat patterns, although the survey responses and Heat Index observations were not spatially or temporally paired. Over 75% and 65% of respondents reported feeling “hot” indoors during the day and at night, respectively, and nearly all described these conditions as “uncomfortable” or “very uncomfortable.” Indoor Heat Index values frequently exceeded outdoor values at night across monitored housing typologies, suggesting limited nighttime thermal relief inside dwellings. Descriptive patterns indicated that indoor heat exposure varied across housing and micro-environmental features such as window size, roof colour, ceiling presence, and nearby vegetation; however, adjusted models did not identify statistically significant housing predictors of indoor Heat Index. Similarly, adjusted logistic regression models did not provide consistent evidence that physical housing characteristics independently predicted heat-related symptoms. Overall, the findings provide local evidence to inform heat-health monitoring, settlement-scale adaptation planning, and future intervention studies.

title: Compounded exposure in sustainable transportation: Identifying the spatial overlap between on-road vehicle emission hotspots and active commuting clusters
abstract: As urban populations continue to grow, rising demand for the movement of people and goods intensifies traffic-related air pollutant (TRAP) emissions, leading to uneven spatial distributions that exacerbate health and socioeconomic disparities. This paper presents a data-driven framework to identify spatial disparities in TRAP emissions and quantify the contribution of each vehicle type to support targeted mitigation strategies. Vehicle-specific emission intensities and spatial patterns are analyzed at the census-tract (CT) level, a geographic unit for statistical analysis, typically encompassing 2,500–8,000 residents. A spatial statistical approach, using image-based traffic data and Moran’s I cluster analysis, is applied to evaluate the distribution of criteria air pollutants and greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions (NO x , PM 2.5 , and CO 2 e) across the city of Surrey, Canada. The framework generates fleet-specific, high-resolution CT-level emission allocations by pollutants, which are used to identify clusters of hot spots. These hot spots are overlaid with active transportation clusters to identify areas where TRAP exposure requires targeted intervention. The framework offers a scalable approach to integrating emissions and equity metrics for equitable emissions reductions. Among the 95 CTs included in the study, five were identified as “double jeopardy” zones, where high levels of walking and cycling activity coincide with elevated TRAP emissions clusters. Passenger Trucks and heavy-duty vehicles (HDVs) are identified as the dominant contributors to emissions within the 14 High-High TRAP tracts. Passenger trucks account for 60% of CO 2 e and 45% of NO x , while HDVs dominate exhaust particulate matter (PM), contributing 57% of PM 2.5.

title: Bikeability index in bike-sharing systems: A dual-level assessment integrating station accessibility and cycling environment
abstract: Understanding and improving the bikeability of urban environments is essential for advancing towards sustainable mobility and reducing the environmental burden generated by short-distance motorized travel. This study proposes a dual-level bikeability index (BI) that integrates large-scale bike-sharing trajectories, built-environment indicators, and spatial–temporal interaction patterns to evaluate urban cycling environments with high granularity and interpretability. A case study is presented using 87,855 dockless bike-sharing trips collected in Xiamen, China. We employ a residual autoencoder with Bayesian optimization to extract compact mobility embeddings that capture user behavior. Emerging hotspot analysis (EHSA) is employed to capture spatial-temporal heterogeneity, while an XGBoost model with SHAP-based interpretation is used to quantify the contributions of land-use diversity, accessibility, road network structure, and weather conditions to bikeability formation. Results show that (i) mixed-use land-use intensity, POI accessibility, and cyclable network proximity are the most influential determinants of BI; (ii) distinct temporal patterns exist between short-distance functional trips and mid-distance recreational trips; and (iii) spatial heterogeneity highlights mismatches between bike-sharing demand and infrastructure provision, particularly in mixed commercial–residential districts. Based on these findings, we provide actionable planning recommendations for station deployment, cycling network enhancement, and demand-responsive operational strategies. This research demonstrates a scalable, data-driven framework for diagnosing urban cycling environments and offers insights that can support evidence-based planning for sustainable cities.

title: SHAP-TAG: Operationalizing explainable AI for urban heat governance through attribution-severity typologies and policy triggers
Smart point cloud–guided 3D gaussian splatting for urban modeling and data-driven analysis
abstract: This paper proposes a combined Smart Point Cloud (SPC) and Smart 3D Gaussian Splatting (S3DGS) framework for integrated urban analysis at block scale. Using laser-scanning point clouds and multi-view imagery of the aula–library heritage block in Netherlands, we first construct an SPC with CityGML-inspired semantics, then train a 3DGS model from the same image set and project SPC labels onto the Gaussians to obtain an S3DGS representation. On this basis, we derive a family of indicators that are usually produced in separate workflows: façade- and ground-plane composition from semantic projections; panoramic exposure metrics for greenery, buildings and sky from renderings of 3DGS with semantic labels (S3DGS); and column- and voxel-based statistics from the segmented SPC. The results demonstrate that the combined SPC–S3DGS model can simultaneously support plan-based, façade-based and view-dependent indicators, and can distinguish coherent scene types such as highly enclosed façade-adjacent zones, tree-dominated corridors, open plazas and mixed transitional spaces. Reflective surfaces and water, which are poorly captured by laser scanning, are recovered through the image-driven S3DGS component. We argue that SPC–S3DGS provides a generic semantic scene representation that can enrich urban digital twins with a visual–environment layer, and that it offers a promising basis for coupling structural, land-cover and exposure metrics in computational studies of computers, environment and urban systems.

title: Wind amplification induced by high-rise buildings and identification of local wind-prone neighborhoods using a CFD-machine learning framework
Surrogate-assisted multi-objective optimization of micro-scale urban tree configurations for heat-stress mitigation with ecological co-benefits
Subtropical climate and intraday temperature variability: Mental health risks and modifying roles of demographic and seasonal factors in Texas
abstract: Objectives To examine the relationships of intra-day hourly temperature variability (HTV) with mental health outcomes in subtropical climates and effect modification by demographic characteristics and season. Methods We applied a time-series meta-analytic framework to analyze daily temperature conditions and hospital visits across the 53 largest Texas counties between 2015 and 2019. A generalized additive model combined with a distributed lag non-linear model was used to examine exposure-lag-response relationships in each region, and a random effects meta-analysis was applied to estimate the pooled effects across counties, followed by stratified analyses to assess effect modification. Results The highest cumulative mental health risks were observed over lag 0-1 days, with increased intra-day HTV associated with higher risks of mental health-related outpatient hospital visits. Compared to young adults, children/youths were at greater risk of outpatient hospital visits for overall mental and behavioral disorders (F00-F99) associated with HTV, whereas older adults showed greater increases in outpatient visits for substance use disorders (F10-F19) in relation to HTV. Additionally, effects peaked at lag 0-1 in most seasons, but winter showed delayed and prolonged cumulative effects. Conclusions The seasonal differences underscore the need to pay particular attention to the heightened risks in spring and prolonged risks in winter. Additionally, greater susceptibility of children/youth and older adults to HTV-related mental disorders suggests that healthcare systems and school-based mental health services should incorporate seasonal monitoring protocols and enhance mental health screening and outreach during high-risk periods of elevated temperature variability in subtropical regions.

title: Interpreting the role of the urban-rural gradient in the spatial variation of heat exposure: Path analysis and nonlinear effects across 24 Chinese megacities
Optimizing summer heat mitigation and equity in urban residential communities: threshold-based evidence from 4678 communities in Chengdu
Mapping urban energy transitions: Decoding solar pv potential, energy burden, and socio-demographic dimensions in the athens metropolitan area
abstract: Urban energy transitions require spatially explicit diagnostics that integrate renewable potential, consumption patterns, and socio-demographic determinants. This study presents a comprehensive framework for assessing rooftop photovoltaic (PV) adequacy, energy burden, and CO₂-equivalent emission savings across all municipalities in the Athens Metropolitan Area (AMA). Using high-resolution three-dimensional radiative modeling and Earth observation datasets, we estimate rooftop PV potential and electricity demand under a deep renovation scenario. Two key indicators—PV adequacy and energy burden—are analyzed in relation to area, population, density, building stock, income, and energy costs. Results reveal strong spatial heterogeneity: municipalities with larger geographic areas and lower population density exhibit higher PV adequacy and lower energy burden, while compact, high-density zones face elevated energy vulnerability. Approximately 24% of AMA households experience energy burden above the 10% threshold, disproportionately affecting 1.2 million residents. Full rooftop PV deployment could yield 1103 kt CO₂ savings, while a modest 10% deployment would halve the number of burdened municipalities. The study delineates targeted, geospatially informed solar planning and aligns with the United Nations’ SDG 7 and SDG 11, offering a transferable framework for sustainable urban planning and equitable energy transitions.

title: Unpacking teleworking benefits: Evidence on mobility demand and carbon emissions
abstract: Teleworking is widely promoted to reduce transport emissions and support climate goals, yet its real-world effectiveness remains uncertain. We combine high-resolution GPS tracking, georeferenced data, app-based daily diaries, and mode-specific life-cycle emission inventories to quantify the mobility and carbon impacts of teleworking. In Spring 2024, we monitored 294 employees in Southern Switzerland over 30 consecutive workdays. A within-subject counterfactual design shows that teleworking reduces daily travel distance by 55% and CO 2 emissions by 47%, primarily through substitution of car-based commuting. Additional non-commuting trips do not meaningfully offset these benefits, indicating no compensation effect. Reductions are larger for long or car-dependent commutes and smaller in transit-rich areas, highlighting the role of spatial context. Social and institutional time constraints, such as childcare and school schedules, affect teleworking impacts by inducing compensatory mobility behaviors. Seasonal and weather conditions further moderate the effects, with warmer days encouraging some additional non-commuting trips. Substitution dominates, and teleworking delivers substantial carbon savings. Our findings provide actionable insights for hybrid work policies, urban sustainability, and decarbonization strategies.

title: Advancing sustainable construction: A trust-enhanced model of AI adoption and realised use
abstract: The transition towards sustainable built environments increasingly depends on the effective integration of AI in construction. While AI can support productivity, safety, decision-making and resource efficiency, its adoption in construction remains fragmented across organisations, projects and professional workflows. This study develops and empirically validates a trust-enhanced Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) to explain AI adoption and realised use in construction. Survey data from 1,233 professionals across Australia, the UK and the US were analysed using structural equation modelling. The model examines the relationships between perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, trust in AI, attitude, behavioural intention and self-reported actual usage. The results show that trust significantly shapes perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness, while behavioural intention is the strongest predictor of self-reported actual AI use. The findings also indicate that trust enables professionals to evaluate whether AI tools are reliable, manageable and useful within project-based workflows. The study contributes to adoption theory by contextualising trust-enhanced TAM within construction, where AI outputs may influence cost, safety, design decisions, site operations and professional responsibility. By modelling realised use rather than behavioural intention alone, the study advances understanding of how AI adoption progresses from perception and intention to reported professional use. The findings provide practical guidance for developing trust-building mechanisms, governance processes and implementation strategies that support responsible, scalable and sustainability-oriented AI adoption in construction.

The potential interface: Urban open spaces system to support urban flood prevention and mitigation
abstract: ABSTRACT Urbanization has significantly transformed natural hydrological cycles, leading to more frequent and severe urban floods, which in turn result in considerable social, environmental, and economic consequences. These effects are closely linked to land-use transformation, soil sealing, and inadequate spatial planning, particularly considering the limited integration between urban drainage systems and open spaces. In response, this study proposes an integrated methodological framework to support urban landscape planning by systematically identifying and evaluating open spaces with the potential to mitigate flood risk through multifunctional uses. The approach combines a quali-quantitative assessment of urban open spaces with hydrodynamic flood modeling, enabling a cross multi-layered spatial analysis of landscape attributes and drainage performance. By vertically integrating these layers, the method identifies interface zones where open spaces can operate as active components of a flood mitigation strategy. The identification of these interface zones supports urban planning and design processes, by incorporating the definition of a multifunctional open space system to enhance flood mitigation capacity and significantly reduce critical flood conditions. Strengthening the role of open and green spaces within the proposed system, this approach also improves environmental performance and contributes to urban quality of life. The proposed framework works as a decision-support tool for urban planning and policy-making, offering a transferable and scalable strategy to promote more resilient and sustainable urban flood management.

title: Identification of heat risk and resilience response in a mountainous megacity from a supply–demand perspective
Flexing electric vehicle charging for socio-technical resilience: Distribution transformer headroom and locational value analyses
abstract: Wide deployment and passive integration of Electric Vehicles (EVs) will have implications on people’s needs, electricity system needs, and costs that could undermine future sustainability efforts. This study highlights the effectiveness of a tripartite tariff structure as a strategic mechanism for shifting electricity demand – especially EV charging – to off-peak periods during both daytime and nighttime hours. Unlike traditional night-only off-peak tariffs, the tripartite model offers a more equitable inclusive approach and helps manage aging urban infrastructure: supporting grid stability needs, achieving cost savings, and enabling greater consumer participation. An evaluation of 5,620 distribution substations of Northern Ireland electricity distribution system revealed that in the absence of flexible EV charging, significant grid reinforcement would be necessary: 66.7% of transformers would require upgrades with one EV per household, increasing to 77.9% with two EVs per household. However, when EV charging is made flexible through the tripartite tariff, upgrade requirements are notably reduced – to 51.9% and 63.0%, respectively. This flexibility results in substantial network upgrade deferrals, amounting to £57.3 million for the one-EV scenario and £59.8 million for the two-EV scenario, with the most significant benefits observed for higher-rated transformers. The findings underscore the need for region-specific strategies in planning EV charging flexibility, as variations in grid capacity, energy resource availability, and policy frameworks can influence outcomes. Additionally, the analysis suggests that transformer upgrades within the distribution system should target capacities of at least 500 kVA, where the impact of demand flexibility becomes more pronounced. Where infrastructure upgrades are necessary, cost-sharing should be equitable, ensuring that customers pay only their fair portion of the required investments.

title: Comparing waterbody cooling during heatwave with subsequent summers in high-latitude coastal Copenhagen
abstract: Due to climate change and urbanisation, urban heat islands (UHIs) and heatwaves are increasingly impacting cities in summertime around the world, including less studied Scandinavian cities. Local cooling effects from waterbodies and tall vegetation exist with large geographical variations, and their dynamics need further attention for understanding their abilities to cool during heatwaves. This study investigates turning points of waterbody cooling effects in coastal Copenhagen (Cfb) on three specific June dates covering a heatwave in 2018, a windier but warm and moist day in 2019, and a colder but moist day in 2020. Significant and consistent cooling effects were found for all three summers, from coastal sea (3.92-4.91°C; 195 m), lakes (1.54-1.96°C; 225 m), especially lakes larger than 4.68 ha (2.81-3.27°C; 165-285 m) and lakes more compact in shape (size/perimeter ≥ 0.0053ha/m) (2.61-3.35°C; 315-375 m). The smaller but significant cooling trends for lakes within proximity to tall vegetation (0.63-1.21°C; 135-225 m) together with observed significantly lower land surface temperatures surrounding this subset of lakes (–0.6-0.8°C) indicate two supplementary but equally important ways for mitigating heat – increasing cooling through larger urban waterbodies and lowering land surface temperatures with tall vegetation. The cooling intensities were lowest on the windy date in 2019, but highest in 2020, indicating limited but significant cooling intensities of dry heatwave waterbody cooling.

title: Electric vehicles and urban sustainability in Europe: Advancing SDG 11 through innovation and infrastructure
abstract: This study presents a fresh outlook on the relation between electric vehicles and urban sustainability in the European Union (EU) and fill the gaps that exist in the current related studies. Firstly, we provided a combined and comprehensive analysis of the influence of electric vehicles, electronic mobility patent, and the prices of electricity on SDG 11.6.2, i.e., the annual mean levels of fine particulate matter (e.g., PM2.5 and PM10) in cities, based on data from 2010 to 2023. Next, we considered some macroeconomic factors such as trade openness, foreign direct investment, economic growth, and population dynamics that were neglected in the literature. The results show that electric vehicles (EVs, BEVs and PHEVs), the inflow of foreign capital, population growth, patents, and publicly accessible recharging facilities are the main drivers for the achievement of sustainable development goal 11.6.2. Besides that, it is recognized that economic growth and the degree of trade liberalization have adverse effects on sustainability goal 11.6.2. We suggested that the decision-makers in the EU should support electronic vehicle adaptation.

title: Spatiotemporal variability and driving mechanisms of urban park cooling effect along an urban-rural gradient: A case study of Shanghai
abstract: Although urban parks play an important role of urban parks in mitigating the urban heat island (UHI) effect, the long-term spatiotemporal patterns and the non-linear, synergistic mechanisms driving their cooling performance across urban-rural gradients remain insufficiently quantified. This study assessed the decadal cooling effects of 210 parks within the Outer Ring Road of Shanghai using summer land surface temperatures temperature data derived from Landsat images (2016–2025). In addition, these long-term observations were interpret with a robust XGBoost-SHAP machine learning framework to explicitly interpret the multidimensional effects of park morphology and land cover. The results showed that while 97.6% of parks exhibited cooling effects during the decade, but marked interannual fluctuations limited stable annual cooling to only ∼67% of parks, and the core cooling metrics showed potential attenuation over time. Spatially, a clear trade-off was observed: parks in the peripheral Outer Ring parks achieved the mean cooling distance (174.79 m), whereas micro-parks in the Inner Ring exhibited the highest cooling efficiency (113.78 m/ha). Moreover, machine learning analysis indicated that optimal cooling is shaped by non-linear thresholds and feature interactions (e.g., Area × Tree cover). Comprehensive cooling performance was optimized when water proportions at ∼10%, building footprints were kept below 25%, and moderately complex geometries were adopted (Shape Index: 1.5–2.0), with tree cover acting as the main positive driver. Overall, this study provides precise, evidence-based thresholds for optimizing park landscape configurations, with highly efficient micro-parks prioritized in dense urban cores and large ecologically dominant parks favored in peripheral areas, to support sustained urban climate resilience.

Using agent-based modelling for investigating the impact of travel behaviour interventions on mode shift: A travel behaviour simulation in Dublin
abstract: The present study examines the impact of various strategic interventions on behavioural changes from private car use to sustainable travel modes in Dublin City, using an agent-based modelling (ABM) approach with a particular focus on soft policy (i.e., cycling promotion campaigns and travel feedback programs) and hard policy (i.e., motor tax and fuel price increments) measures. Utilising the Irish National Household Travel Survey (NHTS), we analysed changes in travel mode share, behavioural stage progression, and CO2 emissions under different policy scenarios. The findings suggest that soft interventions, such as cycling promotion campaigns and travel feedback programs, have consistent impacts on reducing car use, progressing behavioural stages (a shift from lower stages like precontemplation to higher stages like action), and lowering CO₂ emissions, with effects amplified when combined with motor tax and fuel price measures. The findings further highlight that using multiple outcome measures provides a more comprehensive evaluation of the impact, making it valuable for policymakers and decision-makers in assessing different transport policy interventions.

title: Potential impacts of personal autonomous vehicles on travel behaviors: A land use and transportation interaction approach
abstract: This study aims to assess the potential impacts of personal Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) on people’s travel behaviors when vehicle sharing in household and network of friends is allowed. Several hypotheses are developed to address research questions using a simulated environment in the TRANUS land use and transportation interaction (LUTI) framework. To estimate the anticipated effects of AVs, we use the transportation model embedded in this LUTI simulator for the British city of Swindon by analyzing three hypothetical scenarios. Sensitivity analyses are also performed by increasing AV occupancy, speed, and waiting time to test the robustness of the calibrated models and travel demand elasticity of AV deployment. The results indicate that AVs would slightly increase people’s overall travel demand and trip generation by improving accessibility and relocating households to surrounding localities. Meanwhile, AVs are found to reduce overall trip segments by providing seamless and convenient movement and encouraging shared rides. Results also show that AVs are likely to reduce vehicle ownership, vehicle travel distance, passenger hours traveled, vehicle hours traveled, and combined travel costs. It is theorized that these reductions are driven by shrinking solo driving, encouraging shared mobility, lowering empty trips, ensuring seamless passenger transportation, and population exurbanization. In contrast, PKT remains almost unchanged after the introduction of AVs. However, AVs would lead to a decline in public and active transportation use presumably by offering convenience to travelers, reinforcing relocation from inner city neighborhoods, and providing low opportunity cost of travel for outlying communities. Finally, this study offers valuable insights and policy implications for informed decision-making considering the anticipated effects of AVs in transportation systems.

title: Diagnosing urban environmental health in non-attainment cities: a multi-decadal satellite-based framework integrating heat, air pollution and blue-green infrastructure (URBAN-HEALTH - 2000-2024)
Beyond carbon: a systematic review of building decarbonization co-benefits and quantification methods
Co-designing stormwater adaptations through community-informed urban pluvial flood modeling
abstract: The intensification of the hydrologic cycle due to climate change poses a threat to urban areas with aging and under-sized water infrastructure systems which often fail to adequately manage intense storm events. The City of Baltimore, Maryland, experiences recurrent stormwater (pluvial) flooding that overwhelms drainage infrastructure, damages housing and disrupts transportation. Adaptations are urgently needed to manage this threat; however, flood mitigation plans frequently fails to consider the objectives and preferences of residents. Engaging communities in pluvial flood modeling is often limited to hazard identification or model validation, and collaborative development of adaptation strategies is uncommon. This study presents a co-designed urban flood modeling framework in which community and technical experts directly inform flood model development and adaptation design through long-term and iterative engagement. The EPA Storm Water Management Model (SWMM) is used to integrate city-provided drainage infrastructure data, community-mapped flood locations, and local expert knowledge of local hydrologic processes. Three adaptations of interest to stakeholders, including green infrastructure, enhanced maintenance, and a combination of both, are simulated and compared across three representative rainfall scenarios. Enhanced infrastructure maintenance is found to be the most effective adaptation, reducing flood depths at priority intersections, though with spatially variable effects across the watershed. Spatially-concentrated greening provides limited benefit to the watershed as a whole. Together, these adaptations have the potential to reduce flood depths by as much as 55% in select locations, which would greatly reduce impacts on local stakeholders. This work demonstrates that co-produced flood models can serve as shared tools for learning and deliberation. Furthermore, these models can test adaptation options that are grounded in both hydrologic process and community priorities, resulting in more relevant and usable insights for communities working to prepare for climate impacts.

Semantic enrichment of 3D city models via roof material classification for urban greening and heat island mitigation
abstract: HighlightsSemantic Enrichment of 3D City Models via roof-material Classification for Urban Greening and Heat Island Mitigation Semantic enrichment transforms 3D city models from purely geometric representations into information rich systems suitable for spatial analytics. This article addresses a frequently missing but vital attribute in such models, namely roof-material, by combining high resolution RGB image classification with footprint-guided background suppression. Building footprints from OpenStreetMap are rasterized into masks that remove non roof pixels, allowing the classifier to focus on material specific cues rather than surrounding urban context. A lightweight YOLO CLS network is trained to distinguish five roof-material classes. Predicted materials are written back into City Geography Markup Language (CityGML) as per building attributes and then mapped to thermo optical parameters for a streamlined urban heat island screening workflow. This enables estimation of baseline roof temperatures as well as scenario-based changes under cool roof and green roof substitutions. A citywide greening simulation of suitable roof candidates across Hamburg, Germany, indicates an average cooling per greened roof of approximately 0.7 K. The proposed pipeline is data efficient, reproducible, and deployable at city-scale. We evaluate it and quantify potential cooling benefits achievable through standardized roof greening interventions.

title: The association between passenger vehicle size and pedestrian fatality in Australia
abstract: Pedestrian death rate in Australia has increased over multiple consecutive years, following decades of relatively consistent decline, while car-occupant safety has relatively improved. In the United States, this type of divergence has increasingly been linked to the growth of larger passenger vehicles (e.g., SUVs and pick-ups). However, whether this mechanism generalises to other vehicle markets, specifically those with different pedestrian safety histories such as Australia, remains uncertain. Without clear localised evidence, the issue is unlikely to be recognised as a serious safety problem in non-U.S. markets. To assess whether this mechanism operates in Australia, we linked 10,376 pedestrian crashes involving passenger vehicles in Victoria, Australia, over 2012–2025 to actual local vehicle dimension data and analysed how vehicle size — reflected in vehicle weight and height — associates with crash fatality. Our analyses showed that the risk of fatality was 1.2 times higher when the crash involved a station wagon and 1.6 times higher when it involved a utility vehicle, relative to sedans and hatchbacks. Multivariate modelling also showed that, while controlling for other factors, every 100 kg increase in vehicle weight is associated with a 6% increase in pedestrian fatality odds (95% CI: 3% to 10%), and every 10 cm increase in vehicle height is associated with an 11% increase in fatality odds (95% CI: 4% to 18%). The associations were also more evident for crashes occurring at lower speeds. Further modelling suggests that capping vehicle weight and/or height at their median levels corresponds to approximately 9% fewer predicted pedestrian fatalities within the observed crash sample. We conclude that increasing vehicle size could be an important factor associated with pedestrian fatality trends in Australia. The results point to the potential relevance of pedestrian safety concerns raised in the United States to the Australian context, particularly as the local passenger vehicle fleet continue to shift toward larger vehicles. The results also have policy relevance for markets undergoing similar fleet transitions.
