Community thermal energy storage, a cost-effective pathway for the decarbonisation of suburban cooling in Australia
abstract: Residential cooling demand in Australia is increasing due to rising temperatures, urban infill, and improved building insulation that traps internal heat. Solar photovoltaic (PV) generation combined with onsite energy storage presents a promising pathway to decarbonise cooling loads; however, the optimal configuration at a neighbourhood scale remains unclear. This study conducts a comparative assessment of three cooling strategies in a suburban Australian context: (i) individual systems, where each household operates stand-alone PV and storage; (ii) district systems, where cooling and storage are centralised; and (iii) community shared systems, where storage is centralised but households have their own cooling. Each configuration integrates individual PV generation. Energy storage is implemented either as battery storage or thermal energy storage (TES), playing a critical role in enabling load shifting, improving PV self-consumption, and reducing reliance on grid electricity by temporally decoupling cooling demand from solar generation availability. A detailed TRNSYS simulation model was developed using high-resolution meteorological, load, and tariff data for an Australian suburb. System performance was evaluated in terms of energy consumption, primary energy saving, life cycle cost, storage utilisation efficiency, grid export minimisation, PV self-consumption rate, and peak reduction. Among six configurations, the district cooling system with centralised battery achieves the highest primary energy saving (98.6%) and almost eliminates grid imports but also exhibits the highest life cycle cost (USD 1.36 million). In contrast, the community system with thermal energy storage achieved a balanced performance, delivering 86.1% primary energy saving at the lowest life cycle cost of USD 0.55 million, making it the most cost-effective solution for this suburban community. By jointly evaluating individual, district, and community cooling architectures with both battery and PCM storage under a common Australian framework, this study clarifies the techno-economic trade-offs of neighbourhood-scale PV-integrated cooling and highlights community TES as a cost-effective pathway for reducing grid electricity dependence and associated primary energy demand, thereby contributing to the transition towards net-zero energy systems at the suburban scale.

title: Heat and cold at work: Occupational accidents and apparent temperature in the primary and construction sectors across five spanish provinces
abstract: ABSTRACT This study aims to evaluate the impact of Apparent Temperature (AT), a biometeorological index that estimates perceived thermal sensation, on occupational accidents in five Spanish provinces, while separately analyzing accidents in the primary sector (agriculture, forestry, livestock farming, and aquaculture) and construction. An ecological time-series study was conducted over a 17-year period. A Generalized Additive Model combined with a Distributed Lag Non-linear Model using a quasi-Poisson distribution was applied to estimate the association between daily occupational accidents and AT. In the two southern provinces, occupational accidents increase as temperature rises. In contrast, in Ávila, Cantabria, and Pontevedra, the relative risk (RR) of occupational accidents increases at thermal extremes (both low and high AT), although the effect is statistically significant only at low temperatures. In the primary sector, accidents in Cantabria and Pontevedra (the two northern coastal provinces) increase with AT. In Cantabria, the maximum number of accidents occurs at 34°C, where the risk is 1.73 times higher than at 14°C (the AT associated with the minimum number of occupational accidents [ATma]). In Pontevedra, the maximum is reached at 38°C, with a risk 1.48 times higher than at 19°C (ATma). Occupational accidents in construction are statistically significantly associated with AT only in Seville, reaching the highest risk at 40°C, where the risk is 1.38 times higher than at 21°C (ATma). The pattern of association between AT and workplace accidents varies across provinces, which may be influenced by climatic characteristics that, in turn, determine the type of professional activity carried out at different times of the year.

A novel hybrid pay-as-bid market clearing framework for socio-economic sustainability in energy communities
abstract: Energy Communities are a cornerstone of the transition to decentralised urban energy systems, enabling proactive, citizen-led governance to lower procurement costs and maximise collective self-sufficiency. However, traditional energy market paradigms face significant structural difficulties in aligning physical grid management with the socio-economic sustainability required for cooperative urban governance. Conventional marginalist designs trigger an economic investment trap by incrementing local generation prices. In contrast, unconstrained pure pay-as-bid (PAB) designs introduce game-theoretic predation that compromises community equity and accelerates physical network stress. To address this polarisation, this paper presents a novel hybrid PAB mechanism that treats social equity as an operational constraint in smart cities. By embedding collective fairness metrics directly into the clearing engine, the proposed mechanism filters out speculative bidding while structurally guaranteeing a viable revenue stream for asset recovery. The framework is tested across nominal, high-surplus, and energy-scarcity demand scenarios, along with a detailed sensitivity analysis. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed Hybrid PAB framework establishes a unique multi-criteria optimal frontier. Under nominal conditions, it enhances social cohesion by elevating Jain’s Fairness Index by 17.4% to 0.760. During high-surplus contractions, where the marginalist market collapses into a deficit of -0.60 €, the proposed framework successfully reverses this loss into a positive net benefit of 0.56 € while keeping community cost increments strictly bounded at 2.9%. Finally, under energy scarcity stress, where Pure PAB inflates user costs by 7.2%, the Hybrid PAB framework restricts user cost increments to just 1.2% while further elevating collective equity by 8.7% to a peak index of 0.835.

Assessing the effect of window-view distance on mental health and personal well-being in high-density urban environments using city information models and deep learning algorithms
abstract: Urban nature exposure is linked to better mental health and well-being and may support the equigenesis hypothesis that individuals from lower socioeconomic levels may gain more benefits from nature exposure. However, little is known about the effects of window-view distance, which refers to the visual distance from indoor spaces through building windows to surrounding natural or built elements, on mental health and well-being. This is partly due to technical limitations in quantifying window-view distance of buildings at a large scale. This study used photorealistic city information models (CIMs) and computer vision techniques to calculate window-view distance at a large scale in densely built urban environments. It then linked these measurements to the residential locations of participants, along with self-reported data on mental health and personal well-being. Our findings revealed that longer window-view distances were linked to improved mental health and personal well-being. Spatial inequalities were observed at the neighborhood level, with high-income areas typically clustering longer greenery, water, and building view distances, while low-income areas were associated with shorter, more constrained views. Individuals in the lowest income group (monthly household income ≤ 29,999 HKD) may experience greater mental health and personal well-being benefits from window-view greenery distances than individuals in the highest income group (monthly household income ≥ 90,000 HKD), providing partial evidence for the equigenesis hypothesis. The results underscore the necessity of adopting targeted urban planning and housing design strategies that prioritize equitable window-view distance to nature, extending health-oriented planning beyond outdoor provision to the everyday indoor environments where urban residents spend most of their time.

title: Scheduled adaptive recalibration for sustainable and accurate demand forecasting in urban building energy management
abstract: Accurate and adaptive forecasting of urban building energy demand is important for reserve scheduling, demand response, and sustainability-oriented urban energy management. This paper presents an adaptive hybrid forecasting framework that combines a Wasserstein generative adversarial forecaster, particle swarm based hyperparameter adaptation, and validation-calibrated blending with a strong gradient-boosted baseline. The adaptation in this framework is a periodic, scheduled offline recalibration of the forecaster on a daily-to-weekly cadence rather than a real-time, online parameter update; the particle swarm search adjusts a small set of hyperparameters during this recalibration step. The framework is evaluated on a subset of the ASHRAE Great Energy Predictor III dataset covering 20 Panther-site buildings and four forecasting horizons from short-term to medium-term prediction. Across these horizons, the final hybrid performs well on the main absolute-error metrics and consistently improves on the fixed-hyperparameter adversarial baseline, indicating that both adaptation and calibration contribute to forecasting quality. The gains are clearest at the day-ahead and longer horizons, where the method remains competitive with the strongest classical benchmarks. A component-wise ablation attributes most of the relative-error (WMAPE) improvement to the validation-calibrated blend with the gradient-boosted baseline, while particle swarm hyperparameter adaptation contributes a smaller additional gain in absolute error; we therefore frame the adaptation step as a refinement of, rather than the primary source of, the observed gains. Lower forecast dispersion also implies a smaller reserve-related committed energy requirement under an idealized operational planning interpretation; relative to the strong gradient-boosted baseline, this incremental reserve reduction is modest (about 5% in forecast-dispersion terms), whereas the larger headline reduction is measured against the weakest baseline. Overall, the results indicate that adversarial forecasting can provide practical value for urban building energy management when it is combined with explicit adaptation, calibration, and uncertainty-aware evaluation.

title: Urban heat exposure under extreme heatwaves: Decoupling urban form and spatial context effects with GeoSHAP
Spatiotemporal evolution mechanism of urban investment-vitality-carbon efficiency
Relationships between surface urban heat island and vegetation across a regional climatic gradient: the case of southeastern Brazil
abstract: The Surface Urban Heat Island (SUHI) is a well-known phenomenon, but there is no established understanding of how urban and rural vegetation influence it across regional climatic gradients. We investigated the seasonal and regional patterns of daytime land surface temperature (LST), vegetation condition (NDVI), and SUHI across 69 localities distributed along a regional climatic gradient in southeastern Brazil. Using Landsat data corrected for altitude, SUHI was estimated as the difference between median urban temperature and a local cold reference defined by the p5 of LST. Results revealed a regional LST gradient of up to ≂7°C, consistent with near ground air temperature. SUHI intensities were highest during the austral summer (DJF), with median values reaching up to ≂11°C, and weaker during the dry–wet transition season (ASO), with values up to ≂7°C. In summer, when temperature rises and the regional temperature gradient weakens, the dominant driver of SUHI was urban heating, which was therefore more strongly controlled by urban NDVI and its cooling capacity. In contrast, during the dry–wet transition, SUHI was more influenced by non-urban temperature and thus depended on rural NDVI, as seasonal declines in rural biomass increased background temperatures and weakened the urban–rural thermal contrast. Across both seasons, ΔNDVI consistently emerged as a robust predictor of SUHI, highlighting the relational nature of urban surface warming. The SUHI did not show a categorically organized spatial pattern with the regional temperature gradient, but during summer it highlighted clusters of colder locations (< 5°C) in the southeastern sector of the territory, whereas in the far northeastern sector the highest values (> 8°C) clustered together. These results from southeastern Brazil suggest that urban heat mitigation strategies should highlight the role of urban vegetation, particularly during summer—when heat waves are stronger—because of its substantial local cooling capacity.

A LSTM-EGAN framework for forecasting land surface temperature in urban areas based on time-series datasets
abstract: Land surface temperature (LST) is a key parameter for understanding urban thermal environments and is strongly shaped by both historical and contemporary urban land-use patterns. Jointly considering past land-use trajectories and current planning schemes is therefore essential for understanding the spatio-temporal relationships between urban form and LST, and for anticipating the thermal impacts of future development. This paper proposes a spatio-temporal prediction framework based on a Long Short-Term Memory–Enhanced Generative Adversarial Network (LSTM-EGAN) to generate fine-grained LST predictions from urban planning inputs and historical heat maps. Using Istanbul city as a case study, we train the model on a 10-year historical dataset comprising 1600 paired samples constructed from land-use maps, satellite imagery, and LST products. After quantitative accuracy assessment, we conduct scenario-based simulations to explore planning-relevant principles for urban heat mitigation. In addition, we develop an interactive user interface application for future projects. This study proposes a framework and application with the potential to support data-driven urban planning and design under increasing heat stress.

title: Modifying the gravity model based on heat flow patterns to reveal drivers of urban heat and cold corridor intensity
Effects of building layout parameters on wind energy potentials in high-density urban central business district

Phase-resolved impacts of daytime, nighttime, and compound heatwaves on urban air quality in Delhi
The difference between perceived and measured particulate matter in high population density urban environments: A citizen co-creation approach
abstract: Understanding the way citizens perceive air quality and whether these perceptions correlate with actual air quality measurements is important for effective urban planning and policy. The perception-measurement gap and its dependence on context is well known in literature. The perception-measurement gap in dense Mediterranean urban environments remains comparatively less explored. This study aims at identifying the relationship between perceived and measured air quality in the dense urban locality of Gżira (Malta). A co-creative, citizen science approach was used that combines high resolution particulate matter (PM) monitoring with survey based perception and health data. Air quality measurements from nine distributed sensors and a survey of 212 respondents revealed a pronounced mismatch between objective measurements and subjective experience. Annual mean PM 2.5 concentrations ranged from 7.8 to 10.1 μ g /m 3 , while PM 10 ranged from 8.4 to 12.1 μ g /m 3 which are well below European limits (approximately 40%–50% of limits for PM 2.5 and 20%–30% for PM 10 ). Notwithstanding this, a statistical analysis of survey responses indicated high levels of concern and a considerable proportion of the surveyed population associated their environment with negative physical and psychological health impacts. These results highlight that for dense urban environments, the perception-measurement gap may apply and environmental concern may be high despite the relatively small PM pollutant concentrations reported. In these cases, perception may be driven by other factors such as visible urban stressors including traffic and construction activity which were not directly measured in this study. Further work on the perception-measurement gap would be useful by means of more detailed measurements of social and air quality indicators.

title: From asset damage to service disruption: A two-layer cascading flood-risk framework for interdependent infrastructure systems
Urban shrinkage and carbon emission prediction structures: A methodological extension using interpretable machine learning
CausalSolar: Leveraging causal representations of residential solar adoption to enhance image-based detection of rooftop solar panels
abstract: Accurate mapping of residential rooftop solar panels is essential for understanding distributed energy transitions. Conventional image-based models often confuse solar panels with visually similar objects, such as skylights or HVAC units, relying solely on visual cues. Conversely, while existing studies identify demographics, building types, and policy as key drivers of solar adoption, these factors are typically used for ex post explanation of past trends rather than a priori prediction. To bridge this gap, this study introduces CausalSolar, a framework that integrates high-resolution visual learning with a Causal Reasoning Module to enhance residential rooftop solar detection and reasoning. Our framework operationalizes adoption mechanisms across domains of People (PE), Place (PL), Neighborhood Effects (NE), and Regional Effects (RE) as active constraints for object detection. Capitalizing on Conditional Mutual Information (CMI), the framework filters out spurious visual correlations and evaluates rooftop candidates based on both appearance and contextual reality. Applied to 428 census tracts across five North Carolina counties (6,419 km²), CausalSolar achieves an F1 score of 92.91%, outperforming state-of-the-art image-only baselines by 7% to 27%. Beyond detection, our framework characterizes the relative contributions of causal factors that shift along the urban-rural gradient: demographic factors (PE) dominate in dense urban cores and peri-urban neighborhoods, while structural, spatial, and policy cues (PL, NE, and RE) drive detection in moderate- to low-density rural neighborhoods. By embedding socio-behavioral evidence into computer vision, CausalSolar provides an accurate and interpretable tool for large-scale renewable energy mapping and sustainable urban planning.

title: Hourly modeling of urban heat exposure driven by 2D/3D urban form using the urban Tethys-Chloris model
Predictive policy stress-testing for non-motorized transport adoption: A scenario simulation and explainable machine-learning framework. A case study of Kigali city
A dynamic ordinal threshold framework for heterogeneous residential mobility under autonomous vehicle adoption
Unveiling nonlinear dynamics and spatial heterogeneity in urban morphology–land surface temperature relationships: Insights from an interpretable GWRF-SHAP framework across local climate zones
abstract: Urban morphology plays a critical role in shaping urban thermal environments. However, the nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous relationships between morphological characteristics and land surface temperature (LST) remain inadequately quantified, particularly across different local climate zones (LCZs). To address this knowledge gap, this study developed an interpretable geographically weighted random forest framework integrated with SHapley Additive exPlanations (GWRF–SHAP) to evaluate the effects of 2D/3D urban morphological characteristics on block-level LST variations in Xi’an, China. Compared with the conventional RF model, the proposed GWRF model demonstrated superior predictive performance, achieving R² values of 0.718–0.719 and improving prediction accuracy by 9.2–9.9% on test datasets. The results revealed substantial spatial heterogeneity in morphology–LST relationships across LCZs. Urban compactness and imperviousness indicators, including building density (BD), floor area ratio (FAR), and the enhanced normalized difference impervious surface index (ENDISI), generally contributed to higher LSTs, whereas vegetation and water-related indicators, represented by the normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) and modified normalized difference water index (MNDWI), consistently exhibited cooling effects. Furthermore, pronounced nonlinear threshold effects were identified. In compact LCZs, LST increased sharply when BD exceeded approximately 0.27–0.30, while the cooling benefits of vegetation became markedly stronger only when NDVI surpassed critical thresholds ranging from 0.16 to 0.23 in open and sparsely built LCZs. In contrast, building height variability (Hstd) exhibited divergent thermal effects among LCZs, indicating strong context-dependent interactions between urban form and thermal environments. These findings highlight the value of integrating interpretable machine learning with geographically weighted modeling for uncovering complex urban morphology–LST relationships. The proposed framework provides a robust scientific basis for LCZ-specific urban heat mitigation strategies and climate-resilient urban planning.

title: A synthesis of the systemic impact of remote work on greenhouse gas emissions and health
abstract: The widespread adoption of remote working, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, has prompted renewed interest in its broader environmental and health impacts. Now, the partial reversion to traditional work arrangements, raises questions about how remote work can contribute to environmental and health goals in a post-pandemic world. We adopt a systems perspective, integrating findings from recent literature with a causal loop diagram that maps the interdependencies between remote work, transport behaviour, building energy consumption, and healthrelated factors. Using network analysis, we identify key impact pathways and leverage points within this system. Our findings complement the conclusions of existing literature-which indicates that while remote work can reduce commuting-related emissions, these can be offset by increased non-commuting travel and higher residential energy use-by mapping and identifying impact pathways through the system. Office space management emerges as a critical factor in realising energy savings. In terms of health, remote work is associated with increased sedentary behaviour and musculoskeletal issues due to poor ergonomics, how individuals might be affected is strongly dependent on behavioural factors. The systems analysis reveals that the impacts of remote work are mediated by socioeconomic , behavioural, and spatial factors, highlighting the need for integrated policy interventions. We conclude that remote work alone is insufficient to drive substantial environmental or health benefits without complementary measures targeting transport, urban planning, and workplace practices.

title: Estimating the causal effects of landscape interventions on urban thermal environments using generalized random forests
abstract: A growing wave of urban thermal studies has used machine learning models and post-hoc explanation tools, particularly Shapley additive explanations (SHAP), to rank landscape factors and detect nonlinear thermal responses. Yet such predict-then-explain frameworks are designed to explain fitted models rather than real-world interventions, making them vulnerable to spurious correlations, unstable importance rankings, and ambiguous planning implications. This study applies a causal-diagram-informed generalized random forest (GRF) framework to estimate the effects of landscape interventions on land surface temperature (LST) at the city-block scale in Beijing. Built on adaptive local weighting, GRF constructs randomized-controlled-trial-like comparisons among observationally comparable city blocks, enabling the estimation of unit-specific dose-response intervention effects. The results show that replacing impervious surfaces with water bodies, trees, and croplands significantly reduced LST by 0.050 ± 0.023, 0.042 ± 0.011, and 0.034 ± 0.012 °C per 1% increase, respectively, while increasing building coverage raised LST by 0.022 ± 0.014 °C per 1%. Building height, building-height variability, and surface albedo also generated strong cooling effects, whereas all landscape configuration metrics showed no significant effects after accounting for land-cover composition. We also detected strong nonlinear and spatially heterogeneous effects: vegetation, water, and albedo interventions generally showed diminishing marginal cooling returns, and the cooling effects of trees, building-height variability, and albedo were strongest in highly built-up or central urban areas. This GRF workflow can support unit-specific and spatially heterogeneous landscape strategies for targeted urban heat mitigation.

title: Urban resilience association networks in plateau–mountain urban agglomerations from the perspective of differences in resilience-supporting conditions: Structure, mechanism, and vulnerability
Identifying potential vertical spaces for nature-based solutions in dense urban context: GeoAI approach
abstract: Cities worldwide face numerous challenges, including the urban heat island effect, urban stormwater management, and climate change. Nature-based solutions (NBS) can mitigate these impacts, while providing ecosystem services and health co-benefits, yet retrofitting NBS within dense urban fabric is difficult because suitable land is scarce. Underused or unused vertical spaces on building facades and roofs could provide opportunities to increase greenery without competing for ground-level land. However, no existing methodology simultaneously assesses both façade and rooftop vertical spaces for NBS using integrated artificial intelligence and geospatial methods; most studies focus on rooftop greening potential. In this research, we develop and evaluate an integrated GeoAI framework that combines a foundational AI segmentation model applied to street view images for façade greening assessment with a geospatial multicriteria approach for rooftop greening assessment in the dense urban context of Amsterdam. Here, greening potential refers to the physical technical feasibility based on the measurable surface areas' potential for NBS integration. When applied to street-based sampling locations in Mapillary SVI images, our framework achieved a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.74 and a mean F1 (Dice) score of 0.84 for facade segmentation, indicating high accuracy in detecting potential building façade areas. The results suggest high potential for greening building facades in predominantly residential areas, particularly in buildings with few street-facing windows. Additionally, the 10.0 km² of roof area is classified as highly suitable for green roof implementation. Spatial hotspot analysis identified several roof-greening clusters, whereas no such clustering was observed for facades. We provided a replicable workflow for broader implementation of the methodological approach in research and practice, and suggested potential future developments to further assess the vertical greening potential on the unused or underused vertical space above buildings.

title: Erratum to “Quantifying the Spatial-Governance Substitution Effect: A GIS-Integrated Agent-Based Model for Community Public Health Resilience” [Sustainable Cities and Society Volume 149 (2026) SCS_107710]

Corrigendum to “A two-stage GIS–MCDM optimization framework for urban demand-adaptive siting and sizing of hybrid renewable hydrogen facilities” [Sustainable Cities and Society 149 (2026) 107768]
Stochastic flow switching in street intersections
abstract: This study investigates the stochastic nature of turbulent flow switching at street intersections in urban canopies. Direct numerical simulations of turbulent flow over a uniform array of rectangular buildings of height h with a 45° inflow direction reveal bistable switching of horizontal wind direction at heights z = 0.125 h and z = 0.25 h , where the flow alternates between alignment with the short-street (0°) and long-street (90°) axes. The characteristic switching time scale is approximately 10.5 T (where T = h / u τ is the eddy turnover time), with a standard deviation of 3.7 T and a longer residence time in the long-street-aligned state. Wind-tunnel experiments for different idealized urban configurations confirm that this bistable switching is a generic process, with time scales that depend on building geometry and incident wind direction. Analysis of field measurements at a real intersection in London (UK) also shows intermittent bistable switching, indicating that the phenomenon is robust but sensitive to external forcing and building heterogeneity. Flow switching at intersections influences scalar transport, particularly in the near field, where the strongest correlations between wind direction and concentration are found in the adjacent short street. In the far field, these correlations are weakened by increased mixing and street-network-scale interactions. Overall, the findings show that stochastic flow switching is an intrinsic mechanism that shapes urban ventilation pathways and modifies pollutant dispersion patterns, highlighting its relevance for both dispersion modelling and real-world air-quality assessments. With these applications in mind, simple approaches for including this process in street network dispersion models are outlined.

title: From optimal solutions to strategic zones: Nonlinear multi-objective optimization of UGI for mitigating compound carbon–water–heat risks
Space–nature–human associations with land surface temperature across nested planning-spatial units: Evidence from Karst Mountainous Guizhou
abstract: Understanding how urban-spatial, natural, and human-social factors jointly relate to land surface temperature (LST) across nested planning contexts is important for climate-adaptive planning in mountainous cities. Integrated comparisons across planning units that are spatially nested but differ in function, environmental background, and development conditions remain limited. In mountainous karst Guizhou, Southwest China, this study examines the Qianzhong Urban Agglomeration, Guiyang Metropolitan Area, and Gui'an New Area. Hot–cold spot analysis, XGBoost–SHAP, and MGWR are integrated within a space–nature–human (S–N–H) framework to compare LST patterns, model-based variable contributions, nonlinear pairwise interactions, and variable-specific spatial associations under four seasonal–diurnal scenarios. Summer daytime hot spots mainly coincide with built-up areas and development corridors, whereas winter hot spots shift toward western and southern slopes and karst areas; forested mountains and large water bodies remain relatively stable cold spots. Natural-background associations are most prominent in the urban agglomeration, regional gradients coexist with localized built-form and human-activity associations in the metropolitan area, and selected associations become more localized and patchy in the new area, although some remain near-global. S–H, S–N, and N–H interactions vary in direction, magnitude, and response range across planning–spatial and seasonal–diurnal contexts rather than following a uniform cross-level progression. Sensitivity analyses support the principal interpretations across alternative grid resolutions and variable specifications. By linking relative contributions, interaction configurations, and spatial ranges, the framework shifts thermal-environment analysis from isolated factors to context-specific relationships and supports differentiated climate-adaptive planning across nested mountainous planning units.

title: Measuring inclusive social sustainability in aging communities: Development and validation of a holistic, resident-validated social-spatial experience indicator across two Chinese cities
Management and reshaping of urban water supply systems: perspectives from carbon emission reduction
Mapping environmental noise across mainland China using a two-stage stacked ensemble framework
abstract: Rapid urbanization has intensified environmental noise in China, yet a national-scale environmental noise exposure map remains absent. This study developed a two-stage stacked ensemble learning framework to map acoustic environments across mainland China and assess socioeconomic disparities in noise exposure. We integrated 554,948 observations from 103,102 environmental noise monitoring stations with multisource geospatial predictors, including transport networks, land use, population density, nighttime lights, GDP, building footprints, points of interest, air pollutants, meteorological variables, elevation, and vegetation. The modelling framework combined Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost as base learners, followed by a LightGBM meta-learner and residual calibration. The final model achieved an R 2 of 0.660, RMSE of 4.720 dB, and MAE of 3.631 dB at the national scale, with performance varying across regions and urbanization strata. The predicted 1 km × 1 km noise maps revealed spatial and temporal gradients, including higher exposure in eastern urban agglomerations and sustained evening-nighttime noise in metropolitan cores. Population-weighted L den declined across GDP per capita quintiles, whereas the proportion of the population exposed to L den >53 dB was highest in the lower-middle group and declined across the higher quintiles. These findings provide macro-scale evidence of environmental noise exposure and inequality in China and support differentiated strategies for sustainable urban noise management.

title: A hybrid white-box emergy nexus model for endogenous unit emergy value derivation in urban water, energy, and socioeconomic systems

Building density thresholds and urban liveability: Evidence from ordinal logistic modelling in a global south city
abstract: Growing international concern regarding sustainable urban development has shifted scholarly attention from compact urban form toward broader questions of liveability, and urban sustainability. While recent research increasingly highlights the role of density in shaping urban outcomes, empirical evidence from cities of the Global South remains limited, particularly regarding the distinction between building density and population density. This issue is especially important in Iran, where density functions serve not only as a planning instrument but also as a major source of municipal revenue. This study investigates the relationship between building density and neighbourhood liveability in District 9 of Mashhad, Iran, using an ordinal logistic regression framework. A composite liveability index was developed from 30 social, economic, environmental, and physical indicators across 16 neighbourhoods. Building density was measured using Floor Area Ratio (FAR), while liveability was classified into three ordinal categories (low, medium, and high). The results reveal a statistically significant nonlinear relationship between density and liveability (β = 0.0518). Each unit increase in FAR increases the odds of belonging to a higher liveability category by approximately 5.3%, while probability estimates indicate an S-shaped relationship with transition thresholds occurring between FAR values of approximately 500 and 650. The findings further demonstrate that building density and population density should not be treated as equivalent concepts. Higher liveability is associated with planned,of densification, whereas lower liveability is linked to overcrowded and underserved neighbourhoods characterised by high population density despite relatively low building density. The study identifies two contrasting density regimes—a formal, investment-driven regime and an informal, poverty-driven regime—and argues that liveability outcomes are shaped less by density itself than by the governance, and socio-spatial conditions through which density is produced. These findings contribute to debates on sustainable densification, spatial justice, and evidence-based urban planning in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South

title: The green electric vehicle charging station location problem incorporating user choice modeling
abstract: Achieving decarbonization in urban logistics requires promoting the adoption of electric vehicles. In this regard, the strategic location of charging stations plays a critical role. The purpose of this work is to introduce the green electric vehicle charging station location problem, a new problem in which both the technological dimension of sizing the renewable energy systems that supply the charging stations and the behavioral dimension of user preferences for different charging infrastructures are integrated into the same location model. The proposed methodology is applied to a case study using real data from an Italian city, where different policy scenarios are evaluated with respect to factors such as charging infrastructure and environmental and digital awareness. From a policy perspective, the interaction between electric vehicle users and the charging infrastructure is investigated, as well as their willingness to use charging stations powered by clean energy and equipped with wireless charging technologies.

Spatial heterogeneity and landscape associations of urban heat risk under urban expansion in Chinese cities
abstract: Urban heat risk is shaped by the spatial interaction between thermal hazard, population exposure, and vulnerability, yet how long-term urban expansion changes the spatiotemporal distribution of heat risk remains insufficiently understood. This study examined the spatiotemporal evolution of urban heat risk in 15 Chinese cities from 1990 to 2025 using an integrated framework combining hazard, exposure, and a vulnerability index. Dynamic urban boundaries were used to distinguish old urban cores from expansion zones. Nonlinear associations between landscape structure and heat risk were examined across different development stages, and whether the growth of areas classified as high risk followed the pace of urban expansion was assessed. The urban area affected by heat risk increased 5.83-fold, whereas areas classified as high risk increased 3.77-fold, indicating that urban expansion enlarged the overall risk footprint without producing a proportional increase in areas classified as high risk. The population exposed to high thermal hazard increased substantially over the study period, highlighting the increasing concentration of thermal burden among urban populations. Within the adopted composite risk framework, contrasts between high risk and lower risk areas were greater for exposure and the adopted vulnerability index than for hazard. Impervious patch dominance and fragmentation showed stronger associations with composite heat risk in expansion zones, whereas old urban cores showed broader associations involving impervious shape complexity and green space fragmentation. These findings improve understanding of the spatial evolution of urban heat risk during urban expansion and provide insights for heat adaptation strategies tailored to different urban contexts.

title: Mapping heat-sensitive multimorbidity and adaptation mismatch with equity-oriented GeoAI techniques: A dual-scale analysis for sustainable urban climate-health governance
Urban greenness mitigates the negative effect of extreme heat on docked bike-sharing demand: Evidence from Chicago
abstract: Extreme heat is becoming an increasingly severe environmental constraint on low-carbon urban travel. As a travel mode that is directly exposed to outdoor conditions, bike-sharing is especially sensitive to changes in the thermal environment. Although previous studies have examined how thermal conditions affect bike-sharing usage, there is still limited direct empirical evidence on whether greenness around bike-sharing stations can reduce the negative impact of heat on cycling demand. Using Chicago’s docked bike-sharing system as a case, this study constructs a station-hour panel dataset based on approximately 2.3 million valid trip records from May to September 2024. A fixed-effects Poisson pseudo-maximum likelihood model is used to examine the effect of extreme heat on bike-sharing trips and to test whether greenness around stations moderates this effect. The results show that extreme heat hours significantly reduce bike-sharing trips, while higher levels of greenness around stations clearly weaken this negative effect. The predicted decline in trips caused by heat decreases from about 3.8% at low-greenness stations to about 0.2% at high-greenness stations. Robustness checks show that this relationship remains broadly consistent under different heat thresholds and alternative thermal indicators. These findings indicate that the heat sensitivity of bike-sharing usage is spatially uneven and shaped by local environmental conditions. By linking thermal stress, urban greenness, and bike-sharing behavior, this study provides empirical evidence for integrating green infrastructure into heat-resilient mobility planning.

title: Group-specific thermal resilience and retrofit strategies for existing residential buildings under future climate scenarios considering neighborhood effects
Operational challenges of ferry electrification: Scheduling under berth and charging limitations
abstract: In response to growing global commitments to zero-emission public transport, this paper addresses the operational complexities of electrifying ferry systems. Electric ferries introduce unique scheduling challenges due to their high energy consumption, limited battery range, and constrained berth availability. This paper develops a mathematical model to test whether these operational challenges can make electric ferry operation infeasible. Given a ferry network and fixed line headways, this paper proposes a Mixed Integer Linear Program (MILP). The model generates vessel schedules that include line timing, berth assignment, battery charging, crew breaks, and vessel repositioning. To improve tractability over real-world networks, a terminal-timing heuristic is implemented. The objective function is a convex combination of fleet size and rebalancing time. The method is applied to two toy models and to the Sydney ferry network, generating different feasible solutions depending on the weight given to each objective, followed by a discussion on the conditions that make electrification feasible. Results from the Sydney case study suggest that electrification will be operationally challenging under the current berth configuration and realistic charging assumptions, with feasible incumbent schedules showing increased rebalancing and substantial charging-related terminal occupation. Furthermore, for the current Sydney configuration and Auckland-based charging speeds, no feasible solution was found within the computational limit; feasible schedules were obtained only in scenarios with additional infrastructure or faster charging. Overall, the MILP is shown to have sufficient flexibility to study the operational effects of ferry electrification under different scenarios.

Artificial intelligence for generative urban design: A systematic literature review and multi-dimensional framework using large language models
abstract: Rapid urbanization is changing how Artificial Intelligence (AI) enhances urban design processes by reshaping techniques such as spatial planning, parametric modelling, and generative design, leading to greater efficiency, scalability, and adaptability. The primary aim of this SLR is to develop a multi-dimensional framework for researchers and practitioners and to examine the state-of-the-art in AI-based Generative Urban Design (GUD) by extracting and analysing data across multiple dimensions. Adhering to the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis) guidelines, this review employed a novel hybrid screening approach in which large language models (GPT-5 and DeepSeek V3.2) assisted with the initial abstract screening of 612 documents, followed by human cross-validation to ensure accuracy and mitigate algorithmic bias. Manual full-text data extraction was performed on 108 selected documents across five analytical dimensions to perform trend and frequency analyses. The findings map the current GUD ecosystem, revealing critical alignments between AI techniques and the urban design process. The principal contribution of this review is a robust, multi-dimensional framework that guides the development of AI-based GUD digital solutions. It also identifies significant research gaps and limitations within the existing literature, establishing a foundation for future technological innovations alongside ethical considerations.

Wind direction shapes spatial cooling distribution of urban canals: Large-eddy simulation of turbulent and advective heat transport with PALM4U in Amsterdam
abstract: Urban water bodies offer nature-based heat mitigation solutions, yet the mechanistic contributions of turbulent exchange versus advective transport in redistributing canal-induced cooling remain unquantified. We employed PALM4U large-eddy simulation with realistic urban geometry to investigate canal cooling mechanisms in Amsterdam, Netherlands, a dense historic center whose semi-circular canal ring enables systematic study of varying wind-canal orientations within a single setting. Model evaluation against eddy covariance and urban weather station observations demonstrated strong performance for sensible heat flux, net radiation, and near-surface air temperature. Through controlled experiments, we decomposed cooling into turbulent and advective components, revealing that effectiveness depends fundamentally on wind-canal orientation. When wind flows perpendicular to canals, mechanically-driven canyon vortices redistribute cool air from the water surface to surrounding areas, with advection accounting for 60 to 80% of the total cooling effect over adjacent pavement and above the canopy, extending cooling asymmetrically to 2 to 3 building heights vertically and into adjacent canyons. When wind flows parallel to canals, the absence of a cross-canyon vortex limits redistribution, leaving cooling concentrated near the water surface and driven predominantly by local sensible heat flux reduction. Wind-canal orientation does not markedly alter overall cooling intensity but governs how cooling is spatially redistributed within the canopy, producing pronounced thermal heterogeneity, with temperature differences up to 1.5 °C within individual street canyons. While these magnitudes reflect a single summer day and Amsterdam’s specific morphology, the mechanism points to a transferable principle: orienting blue infrastructure relative to prevailing summer winds can steer cooling toward pedestrian spaces.

title: Operational building CO₂ emissions and grid-level functional mixedness in Chinese cities
UAV-enabled intelligent curbside monitoring: A lightweight end-to-end framework for sustainable urban parking governance
Towards thermal health equity for vulnerable populations: Thermal comfort of pregnant women across gestational stages in hospital environments
abstract: Optimal thermal comfort for pregnant women in hospital environments is crucial due to their unique physiological conditions, yet research addressing their specific needs, especially changes in metabolism across pregnancy stages, is still limited. This study examined the thermal comfort of pregnant women and their accompanying individuals in hospital outpatient waiting areas over a full year in a cold zone of China, encompassing both heating and cooling seasons. A total of 2,068 questionnaires were collected, combining subjective thermal sensations with objective environmental measurements. Findings revealed that basal metabolic rate (BMR) adjusted PMV models improved prediction accuracy for pregnant women, with a 6.60% improvement observed in late pregnancy. Neutral temperatures declined with pregnancy progression, from 23.3°C to 21.6°C in the cooling season and 21.0°C to 20.3°C in the heating season, indicating increased heat sensitivity in later stages. Preferred temperatures remained relatively stable (21.1-21.8°C), while thermal sensitivity increased with pregnancy progression (Probit slopes from 0.39 to 0.61). Furthermore, adaptive PMV models (aPMV and ePMV) outperformed the standard PMV across all studied groups. The overlap of thermal comfort zones indicated seasonally adaptive temperature ranges: 20.4-24.6 °C during the cooling season, 17.6-24.8 °C in the heating season, and 17.7-24.0 °C throughout the year. Participants also preferred a relative humidity range of 40% to 65% and gentle airflow to enhance their perception of freshness. These insights offer valuable guidance for occupant-centered design and ventilation strategies in healthcare settings and contribute to the refinement of thermal comfort standards.

title: An agent-based approach for the adoption of renewable energy communities in urban districts
abstract: The energy transition is fostering decentralised configurations of energy production such as the Renewable Energy Communities (RECs), in which prosumers aggregate to maximise collective self-consumption and local benefits. Their adoption dynamics remain underexplored, especially the combined role of technical, economic and social drivers in enrolment decisions. This study develops an agent-based model couple with Urban Building Energy Modelling outputs to simulate REC adoption in a mixed-use district over 20 years. The decision-making is based on a multi-criteria and two-level weighting utility function that accounts for financial, environmental, and social dimensions and compares three energy-market mechanisms, representing each household and non-residential building as an agent. At each monthly step, agents first evaluate the feasibility of photovoltaic investment and, if viable, choose between remaining individual prosumers or probabilistically joining a REC under three policy mechanisms: Virtual Energy Sharing (VES), Peer-to-Peer (P2P) and Community Net Metering (CNM). Results show that the three mechanisms generate similar enrolment trajectories, with peak adoption occurring between years 4 and 8, which leads to different outcomes for installed PV capacity, local self-consumption and revenue generation. CNM maximises local self-consumption of 668 MWh/y based on virtual credits but produces no sharing revenues and exhibits declining long-run utility scores; VES achieves the highest cumulative PV capacity with 726 kW p and more than 28 k EUR/y stable revenue; P2P pricing volatility related to internal dynamic pricing may prevent large-rooftop members, yielding only to 535 kW p PV installed. This framework allows the exploration of how policy designs shape the real-world diffusion of RECs, thereby highlighting the interplay between economics, technology, and social behaviour in the context of energy transition.

title: Street tree cooling is modulated by the built environment: fine-scale evidence from mobile measurements
abstract: Increasing urban tree cover, a widely adopted approach for mitigating urban heat, is often challenged by the difficulty of designing cities that are both compact and green. Street trees provide a unique opportunity to integrate trees directly into the existing fabric of cities, only requiring a small permeable spot for planting. However, many cities are highly heterogeneous in their form, such as with variable building heights and surface characteristics. This heterogeneity can affect local microclimate conditions via changes to both amount of incoming radiation and local heat transfers. As the processes underlying the cooling properties of trees are directly affected by the local microclimate, the cooling potential of urban street trees may vary depending on the surrounding urban form. We use a high-frequency bike-based mobile measurement system to collect fine-scale air and ground surface temperature measurements within the densely built and mostly impervious area of downtown Montréal, Canada. We measure variation in daytime and nighttime temperatures across a range of urban microclimate conditions using a stratified transect survey analysis of temperatures at pedestrian height. Our analysis demonstrates that street trees cool daytime air temperature about three times more in areas with high building obstruction compared to open areas, while the cooling effect on daytime ground surface temperature remains consistent regardless of the surrounding built environment. At night, however, higher canopy cover led to slightly warmer air temperatures in open areas. Overall, these results support street trees as valuable nature-based solutions to mitigate extreme heat, even in highly dense urban environments.

MTML-EV: Multi-target meta-learning for cross-zone urban electric vehicle charging infrastructure management
abstract: Rapid electric vehicle (EV) adoption is reshaping urban mobility and energy systems, intensifying challenges for charging infrastructure management, including congestion, uneven spatial demand, and grid stress. Addressing these challenges requires reliable forecasting of multiple charging-system states across both near-real-time operation and short-term planning horizons, particularly for newly deployed or evolving zones with limited historical data. Existing urban EV charging forecasting approaches often focus on individual charging-system variables and exhibit limited adaptability to previously unseen zones. To address this limitation, this paper presents MTML-EV, a multi-target meta-learning framework that jointly predicts charging occupancy, energy demand, and electricity price across 1-, 6-, and 12-hour forecasting horizons. MTML-EV formulates each traffic zone as a learning task and leverages a BiGRU-based temporal encoder optimized with first-order model-agnostic meta-learning (FOMAML) to learn transferable temporal representations that enable rapid adaptation to previously unseen zones. Extensive experiments on the UrbanEV benchmark evaluate MTML-EV across multiple forecasting horizons and unseen-zone adaptation scenarios against deep learning, hybrid, and Transformer-based baselines. For 1-hour ahead prediction on unseen zones, MTML-EV reduces RMSE by 7.5% for energy demand and 59% for electricity price compared with the strongest Transformer baseline while maintaining high occupancy forecasting accuracy. Additional robustness analyses across multiple unseen-zone partitions demonstrate that these performance gains remain stable under varying zone configurations, while interpretability analysis confirms that the model relies on meaningful temporal, charging-related, and contextual factors. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of MTML-EV for multi-target cross-zone forecasting under heterogeneous urban conditions, highlighting the value of transferable temporal representations for adaptive EV charging infrastructure management.

title: Public support for AI-enabled local government services: Governance context, AI modality, and algorithmic targeting
abstract: AI is increasingly embedded in local government systems, shaping how cities organise, automate, and govern public services. However, public support for AI-enabled services remains uneven across governance contexts, raising critical questions for responsible and sustainable urban innovation. This study investigates how citizens in Australia, Hong Kong, and Saudi Arabia evaluate different AI modalities in municipal service delivery, and how these evaluations vary depending on the populations targeted by algorithmic systems. Drawing on a cross-country scenario-based survey (n = 1,183) incorporating six AI service scenarios, the findings suggested three key patterns. First, public support varies significantly across governance contexts, with consistently higher acceptance in Saudi Arabia, greater variability in Australia, and more cautious attitudes in Hong Kong. Second, general, lower-sensitivity scenarios were evaluated more favourably than individually targeted scenarios, although targeting co-varied with service purpose and sensitivity. Third, perceptions differed across modality-based scenario types: scenarios involving image recognition were rated more useful, chatbots as more human-like, and scenarios using predictive analytics in local services received lower support. These findings demonstrate that public acceptance of AI in local government is shaped critically by who the technology is applied to and what the personal consequences are. They contribute to responsible and sustainable urban AI governance by showing that public support depends not only on technical capability, but also on perceived fairness, accountability, and contextual fit.

title: Dynamics of urban cooling strategies across distinct climatic contexts: A scoping review and evidence analysis
abstract: The paradigm of the contemporary global scenario is characterized by accelerated urban expansion. This expansion promotes soil sealing and the replacement of vegetation with low-albedo materials, thereby intensifying the Urban Heat Island effect, which elevates temperatures by 2 °C to 12 °C. By means of a scoping review structured under the PRISMA-ScR protocol and complemented by bibliometric analysis (2015-2025), this study systematized 86 articles to map and evaluate the performance of urban cooling strategies across different climate classifications. The results indicate an exponential growth in investigations, although a concentration in subtropical and continental climates was detected, with a research prominence from China. It was found that the effectiveness of Nature-Based Solutions is not a constant attribute, as it is conditioned by urban configuration. An asymmetry in efficacy was evidenced: while parks and dense afforestation attenuate the Physiological Equivalent Temperature index by up to 18 °C, green roofs exhibit limited performance at the pedestrian level (0.1 °C to 0.7 °C). This discrepancy corroborates that the operative effectiveness of these strategies transcends the typology of the technology, depending instead on morphological arrangement and configuration. The study highlights critical trade-offs, such as the increase in Mean Radiant Temperature induced by high-albedo materials in compact urban canyons and the physiological limitations of vegetation under water stress conditions in arid climates. It is inferred that heat mitigation requires multiscale approaches and bioclimatic contextualization, rendering the expansion of the knowledge frontier in the Global South imperative to ensure urban resilience in the face of climate change.

title: Inferred vertical coupling of urban heat islands across morphology zones: conditional effects and planning implications
abstract: Understanding the three-dimensional structure of the urban heat island (UHI) is essential for climate-adaptive planning. Beyond surface and canopy-layer warming, UHIs involve vertically integrated heat accumulation; however, most studies assess temperature differences at a single height. This study infers vertical UHI coupling from the joint yet differentiated responses of surface (SUHII), canopy-layer (CUHII), and vertically integrated boundary-layer (VUHII) indicators, without directly quantifying coupling or simulating energy exchange. It further examines morphology-dependent relationships using morphology-zone classification and double machine learning (DML)-based statistical attribution. The results show that SUHII and CUHII exhibit continuous urban-rural gradients, whereas VUHII is more localized and fragmented. At night, mean VUHII reaches 963.5 K·m in dense central districts, compared with 206.6 K·m in peripheral plains, indicating that conventional surface- or canopy-layer metrics alone may not fully represent vertically integrated heat accumulation within the lower atmosphere. Thermal intensity generally follows high-rise compact (HC) > low-rise compact (LC) > low-rise sparse (LS) > low-rise open (LO). Nighttime VUHII trends are 59.1, 18.8, and 13.1 K·m·a⁻¹ in HC, LC, and LS zones, respectively, and winter nighttime VUHII exceeds 2500 K·m in HC zones. Transition-zone analysis indicates that VUHII changes lag behind those of SUHII and CUHII during urban-form evolution: during LS to HC transitions, VUHII remains 200–400 K·m, far below the 1500–2000 K·m observed in stable HC zones. After adjustment for observed covariates, DML-based statistical attribution indicates that land cover and surface properties have the strongest estimated conditional associations with SUHII and CUHII. In contrast, VUHII is more strongly associated with three-dimensional urban structure, atmospheric conditions, and human activity. At night, building-height heterogeneity, impervious-surface connectivity, and population density show positive conditional effects on VUHII, whereas vegetation shows a negative conditional effect. These findings provide evidence-informed planning priorities for morphology-aware mitigation of heat accumulation.

Identifying and connecting green space demand areas for urban heat island mitigation: A spatial localization planning approach
Beyond local climate zones: Continuous morphology archetypes for heat mitigation across 66 cities
abstract: Urban block morphology is fixed at masterplan stage and locks in pedestrian-level thermal performance for 50–100 years, yet design-stage guidance for climate-smart morphology remains poorly generalised. Most published analyses are single-city, and the cross-city literature relies predominantly on Local Climate Zone categorical classes that collapse within-class morphology variance. We address this gap with a measurement-first multi-city framework (prioritising harmonised empirical measurement over categorical assumptions) built on a rigorous, fully open data stack: 33 715 cloud-masked one-square-kilometre patches harmonised across 66 cities and 15 major Köppen climate zones (33 498 retained after a physical-plausibility quality screen on the surface-UHI target), pairing 3-summer rolling-mean Landsat 8/9 surface-temperature anomalies with continuous morphology features extracted from the latest open global building-footprint-with-heights products (Microsoft Global ML, Google Open Buildings v3, GlobalBuildingAtlas, GLAMOUR), an ESA WorldCover land-cover mask, ERA5-Land summer air temperature, WUDAPT LCZ, and SRTM elevation. A linear mixed-effects model with city random intercept attains a marginal R2=0.25 on the within-city-centred UHI target and a conditional R2=0.39 (ICC =0.18); all 8 morphology features are statistically significant at the 95% level, though morphology still explains only a limited share of total surface-UHI variability, with climate and synoptic context dominant. Tree-canopy fraction is the dominant cooling lever (β=−0.64, p<10−122); water fraction (β=−0.58), 80th-percentile NDVI (β=−0.31), building-height coefficient-of-variation (β=−0.18) and mean building height (β=−0.09) also cool, while bare-soil (β=+0.42) and built-up (β=+0.31) fractions are the dominant warming factors. Per-zone mixed-effects models lift the patch-weighted pooled marginal R2 to 0.38, reaching 0.55 in Dwa and 0.51 in Dfb and Cwb. Tree-canopy fraction is the only universal lever, with a negative coefficient in all 14 zones and significance in 13. We extract 144 empirically Pareto-optimal patches in (UHI, density) space and cluster them into three exploratory climate-smart archetypes (silhouette =0.38). The harmonised patch-level table, ingest-to-archetypes pipeline, and archetype card library are released under an open licence.

title: Prioritising nature-based solutions for urban flood mitigation in public and private spaces: A study in Trento, Italy
abstract: Urban flooding is a hydrologic–hydraulic phenomenon influenced by climate change and driven by intense urbanization. Nature‑Based Solutions (NBS) can help mitigate this phenomenon by providing water‑regulating ecosystem services. NBS spatial prioritisation is increasingly used to identify which interventions should be implemented and where. However, most existing approaches are based on simple hydrologic analyses of surface runoff that overlook hydraulic pressure within the sewer system. Moreover, opportunities for NBS implementation are often assessed without distinguishing between public and private spaces, thus missing key information for decision-making. This study develops and tests a spatially explicit method at the subcatchment level that combines three hazard-contributing indicators (Runoff Coefficient, Flooding Ratio and Surcharging Ratio), with suitability analysis for different NBS types in both public and private spaces. The testing application in Trento, Italy, shows that green roofs, rain gardens, and permeable pavements generate distinct priority patterns. The three indicators capture complementary and spatially heterogeneous hazard contributions of subcatchments. Results also highlight that private areas suitable for NBS implementation recur more often in subcatchments classified as high priority under multiple hazard-contributing indicators, whereas suitable public areas are fewer and predominantly associated with a single indicator. By combining hydrologic and hydraulic hazard contribution with public and private suitability for NBS implementation, the study provides a spatially‑explicit prioritisation tool for urban planning, translating hazard contributions into spatial priorities to identify where different NBS types should be most appropriately targeted within the urban fabric.

title: Diagnosing peer-group misfit in registry-based urban building energy benchmarks
